title: When the Middle Ages were
description: The Middle Ages run from the collapse of Roman rule in the West in the 5th century to the Renaissance: roughly 500 to 1500, about a thousand years.

facts.text: The Middle Ages is the period of European history from the collapse of Roman civilization in the 5th century CE to the Renaissance.
The Middle Ages are traditionally dated from about 500 to 1400-1500 CE, roughly a thousand years.
The Renaissance is variously dated as beginning in the 13th, 14th or 15th century, depending on the region of Europe.
The usual marker for the start of the Middle Ages is 476, when the last emperor in the West was deposed, the traditional end of the Western Roman Empire.

title: Early, high and late
description: Historians divide the Middle Ages into early (about 500-1000), high or central (about 1000-1300) and late (about 1300-1500) periods.

facts.text: Historians often divide the Middle Ages into early, central or high, and late periods.
The early medieval period of western Europe ran from about 500 to 1000, a time of frequent warfare when town life virtually disappeared.
The Late Middle Ages is dated from about 1300 to 1500.

title: Why "Middle" Ages
description: Renaissance scholars invented the Middle Ages as a gap between classical antiquity and their own revival; medieval means "middle age".

facts.text: Italian scholars of the Renaissance created the idea of the Middle Ages to set their own era, a revival of classical learning, apart from the thousand years before it, which they cast as darkness and ignorance.
The word medieval comes from Latin medium, "the middle", and aevum, "age".
The 14th-century Italian scholar Petrarch wrote of living in a dark time that had begun with the decline of the Roman Empire.

title: The "Dark Ages" debate
description: Historians now rarely use "Dark Ages" because it passes a negative judgment on a whole era; evidence shows the period was not dark.

facts.text: The term "Dark Ages" is now rarely used by historians because of the value judgment it implies.
"Dark Ages" is sometimes taken to mean a lack of information about the period, but its usual sense is a time of intellectual darkness and barbarity.
Archaeological finds such as the Sutton Hoo ship burial have shown the sophistication of a period once dismissed as the "Dark Ages".

title: 476: a convenient line
description: Odoacer deposed the last western emperor in 476, the traditional end of the Western Roman Empire, but he ruled as king and Roman government carried on.

facts.text: In 476 the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor in the West; 476 is traditionally considered the end of the Western Roman Empire.
Odoacer called himself king, not emperor, and recognized the eastern emperor, Zeno, as his overlord.
Under Theodoric, the Romans of Italy were still governed by the old Roman civil service, which carried on more or less unchanged.

title: Kingdoms after Rome
description: Germanic kingdoms replaced Rome in the West: Ostrogoths in Italy, Visigoths in Spain, Vandals in North Africa, Franks in Gaul, Anglo-Saxons in Britain.

facts.text: After losing most of their lands in Gaul in 507, the Visigoths ruled a kingdom in Spain with its capital at Toledo, until Muslim forces destroyed it in 711.
The Vandals took Carthage in 439 and ruled a kingdom in North Africa until Justinian's general Belisarius destroyed it in 533-534.
By about 500 the Franks ruled northern Gaul, and Angles, Saxons and Jutes were settling in Britain.
Theodoric's Ostrogoths and the Visigoths were Arian Christians, not Catholics.
The Ostrogoth king Theodoric invaded Italy in 489, killed Odoacer in 493 and ruled Italy as king until 526.
In Theodoric's Italy only Goths served in the army, while Romans ran the civil government.

title: The Byzantine Empire
description: The eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until 1453; its Greek-speaking people called themselves Romans.

facts.text: The Byzantine Empire, the eastern half of the Roman Empire, survived for about a thousand years after the western half and fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.
The empire's people called themselves Romaioi, Romans; the modern name Byzantine comes from Byzantium, the old Greek colony where Constantinople was founded in 330.
Over time, Greek replaced Latin as the language of the eastern empire's government.

title: How Byzantium lasted
description: Constantinople's layered land walls and a trusted gold coin, the solidus, helped the eastern empire survive for centuries.

facts.text: Constantinople's land walls, begun under Emperor Theodosius II in 412, combined a moat, an outer wall and a main wall with 96 towers.
Constantinople's walls held firm in the early Middle Ages against Germanic, Hun, Avar, Slav and Arab attackers; the city finally fell to Ottoman forces armed with heavy artillery in 1453.
The Byzantine gold coin, the solidus (called the bezant in the West), weighed about 4.5 grams, was known for its purity for centuries and dominated European trade until the 13th century.

title: Justinian's law code
description: Justinian had centuries of Roman law sorted into the Corpus Juris Civilis, which became the foundation of civil law in continental Europe and Latin America.

facts.text: Justinian I ruled the Byzantine Empire from 527 to 565.
Between 530 and 533, a commission of 16 lawyers led by Tribonian compiled the Digest of Roman legal writings, published in 50 books.
Justinian's code rationalized hundreds of years of Roman law: contradictions were removed, and laws left out of it were repealed.
Justinian's collections of law are known together as the Corpus Juris Civilis, the "Body of Civil Law".
Roman law, through Justinian's code, became the foundation of civil law, the legal system used today in continental Europe and throughout Latin America.

title: Hagia Sophia
description: Justinian's great church, built 532-537 after a riot burned the old one, with a vast dome that seems to float.

facts.text: After the Nika riots burned the earlier church in January 532, Justinian had Hagia Sophia built; it was completed in 537.
Hagia Sophia, meaning "Holy Wisdom", was designed by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidorus of Miletus.
Hagia Sophia's main dome is about 32 meters across, and windows at its base hide the supports in daylight, so the dome seems to float.
The historian Procopius wrote that the dome seemed "suspended from heaven by that golden chain".
For nearly a thousand years, Hagia Sophia was the largest cathedral in Christendom.

title: Clovis and the Franks
description: Clovis united the Franks, conquered most of Gaul and became a Catholic Christian, which won him the support of the bishops and most of his subjects.

facts.text: The Franks were a Germanic-speaking people, and the name France comes from their name.
The Franks built the most powerful Christian kingdom of early medieval western Europe.
A form of Clovis's name, Louis, became the most common name of French kings.
Clovis was king of the Franks from 481 to 511, and in 486 he took over the last Roman-ruled territory in Gaul.
Clovis forced the other Frankish groups to accept his rule.
In 507 Clovis defeated the Visigoths and took Aquitaine, in southwestern Gaul.
Clovis made Paris the capital of his kingdom.
Clovis, whose wife Clotilda was a Catholic, was baptized a Catholic Christian at Reims by Bishop Remigius; the date is debated, with dates given including 498 and 508.
Clovis's Catholic conversion won him the support of the church and of the Catholic majority he ruled, and spared Gaul the long conflicts seen in other Germanic kingdoms.
When Clovis died in 511, his kingdom was divided among his four surviving sons; his Merovingian dynasty lasted more than 200 years.

title: Benedict's Rule
description: Benedict of Nursia's Rule balanced prayer, work and reading, and became the standard for monasteries across western Europe.

facts.text: In 529 Benedict of Nursia founded his monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy.
The Rule of St. Benedict balanced prayer, work and study, with about five hours of manual work and four of reading scripture and spiritual writings a day, plus enough food and sleep.
By the early 9th century, the Benedictine Rule had replaced most other monastic rules in northern and western Europe.

title: Monks and books
description: In the early Middle Ages, monks copied books by hand in scriptoria, and figures like Cassiodorus made sure pagan classics were copied too.

facts.text: Copying was hard work; medieval scribes often said, "Two fingers hold the pen, but the whole body toils."
In the early Middle Ages, books found refuge in monasteries, where they were copied by hand.
Monks needed service books, Bibles and the writings of the Church Fathers, which meant much time spent copying manuscripts.
A scriptorium was a writing room set aside in a monastery for scribes copying manuscripts.
Medieval books were written on parchment or vellum, prepared from animal skin.
Cassiodorus, a senior official under Theodoric, founded the monastery of Vivarium around 540 and had its monks copy pagan as well as Christian authors, an example later followed elsewhere.
Book production was so slow that a monastic library of 600 volumes was considered fairly large.

title: How Islam began
description: Muhammad, born in Mecca about 570, preached what Muslims believe are revelations from God, gathered in the Qur'an; the move to Medina in 622 begins the Islamic calendar.

facts.text: Muhammad was born around 570 in Mecca, in Arabia.
By tradition, Muhammad had a vision of the angel Gabriel in 610; Muslims believe the Qur'an is the word of God, revealed to him in stages through Gabriel.
In 622 Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina; this move, the hijra, marks the start of the Islamic calendar.
Muhammad died in Medina in 632.

title: The first caliphates
description: Caliphs ("successors") led the Muslim community after 632; within about a century their empire stretched from Spain to the Indus.

facts.text: After Muhammad's death, leaders of the Muslim community were called caliphs, from khalifah, "successor".
Under the first four caliphs (632-661), Arab Muslim armies beat the Byzantines at Yarmuk in 636, took Syria and Egypt from them, and defeated the armies of Persia.
The Umayyad caliphs (661-750) moved the capital from Medina to Damascus.
Under the Umayyads, Muslim forces took North Africa and, from 711, overran most of the Iberian Peninsula.
By the early 8th century, the caliphate stretched from Spain to Central Asia and the Indus River valley.
Conquered Christians and Jews, whom Muslims called People of the Book, could keep their religion as long as they paid taxes to the new government.

title: Anglo-Saxon England
description: Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled Britain after Roman rule ended and built several kingdoms; the Angles gave England its name.

facts.text: The Anglo-Saxons were Germanic peoples, chiefly Angles, Saxons and Jutes, who ruled much of what is now England from the 5th century to the Norman Conquest of 1066.
Roman rule in Britain ended about 410, and archaeology suggests some Germanic migrants arrived even before that.
Anglo-Saxon kingdoms included Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Sussex, Wessex and Kent.
The name England comes from Old English Engla land, "land of the Angles".

title: Sutton Hoo
description: The 1939 ship burial at Sutton Hoo, probably King Rædwald's, revealed a rich, well-connected Anglo-Saxon world.

facts.text: Landowner Edith Pretty hired local archaeologist Basil Brown, who found the Sutton Hoo ship burial in Suffolk in May 1939.
The ship's wood had decayed, but its iron rivets and outline in the sand showed a ship some 27 metres long.
No body was found; later chemical analysis suggested it had dissolved in the acidic soil.
The burial held 263 finds of gold, garnet, silver, bronze and other materials, including a famous helmet and objects from Byzantium.
The burial is usually thought to be that of Rædwald, king of East Anglia, who died around 624.
Edith Pretty donated the whole Sutton Hoo treasure to the British Museum in 1939.
The discovery reshaped understanding of Anglo-Saxon England, showing the sophistication of a period once dismissed as the "Dark Ages".

title: Rome's three heirs
description: After Rome fell in the West, its world passed to three heirs: the western kingdoms, the Byzantine Empire and the caliphate.

facts.text: Historians describe the old Roman world after about 500 as passing to three heirs: the Byzantine Empire, an Islamic empire, and the western European kingdoms that looked to the Roman Church.

title: Charlemagne's empire
description: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768 to 814, came from the family that replaced the Merovingians and conquered much of western Europe.

facts.text: Charlemagne, whose name means Charles the Great, was king of the Franks from 768 until his death in 814.
In 751 Charlemagne's father, Pippin III, took the Frankish throne from the last Merovingian king.
Charlemagne became king of the Lombards, in Italy, in 774, and fought the Saxons for about 30 years until they submitted in 804.
By the end of his reign, Charlemagne's realm covered much of western Europe.

title: The Carolingian Renaissance
description: Charlemagne revived learning: Alcuin ran his palace school, scholars copied classical texts, and a clear new script shaped the letters we read today.

facts.text: In 781 Charlemagne invited the English scholar Alcuin of York to head his palace school at Aachen.
In the Carolingian Renaissance, scholars copied large numbers of classical Latin texts, many of which might otherwise have been lost.
Under Charlemagne, monasteries and other church institutions added schools.
Carolingian minuscule, a clear script of Charlemagne's reforms, was revived by Renaissance scholars and is the basis of today's roman type.
Einhard wrote that Charlemagne kept writing tablets under his pillow to practise his letters, but began too late in life to succeed.

title: Emperor in 800
description: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor, reviving the title in the West, angering Byzantium and making popes the makers of emperors.

facts.text: In 799 Pope Leo III was attacked in Rome and fled to Charlemagne, who had him restored as pope.
On Christmas Day 800, in St Peter's Basilica in Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans.
The coronation restored an emperor in the West for the first time since the empire there dissolved in the 5th century.
Einhard wrote that Charlemagne would not have entered the church that day had he known the pope's plan; historians debate this.
The coronation set a precedent: from then on, emperors in the West would be crowned by popes.
The Byzantines regarded Charlemagne as a usurper of the Roman imperial title, beginning a long rivalry between East and West.
In 843 the Treaty of Verdun split Charlemagne's empire among three grandsons, foreshadowing western Europe's countries, France among them.

title: Who the Vikings were
description: The Vikings were Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled from the late 8th century; most were farmers, and the Age is dated from the Lindisfarne raid of 793.

facts.text: The Viking Age is usually dated from 8 June 793, when raiders attacked the monastery on Lindisfarne, the first documented Viking attack.
Lindisfarne is an island off the coast of north-east England.
Monasteries made tempting targets for Vikings: they held church silver and were less well defended than trading towns.
Alcuin, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote after Lindisfarne that never before had such terror appeared in Britain.
Vikings were Scandinavians, from what are now Denmark, Norway and Sweden, active from the late 8th century to the 11th.
Most Vikings were farmers living in small villages of six or seven farms; only a small share lived in towns.
Vikings abroad could be traders, explorers, settlers and mercenaries as well as raiders.
Silver coins minted in Muslim Central Asia reached Viking-Age Denmark by trade along the rivers of Russia.

title: No horns
description: Vikings did not wear horned helmets: the best-preserved Viking helmet has none, no Viking-age writer mentions them, and the image came from 19th-century artists.

facts.text: The best-preserved Viking Age helmet, from a warrior's grave at Gjermundbu in Norway, has no horns.
No writer of the Viking Age mentions Vikings wearing horned helmets, and horns would have got in the way in battle and on crowded ships.
The image of horned Viking helmets was popularized by 19th-century artists.

title: Viking longships
description: Clinker-built longships with a square sail and oars drew so little water that they could run onto beaches, go up rivers and be dragged overland.

facts.text: Alcuin wrote that no one had thought "such an inroad from the sea could be made".
Longships were clinker-built, with overlapping planks fastened together, sturdy in heavy seas, and pointed at both ends.
A longship carried one large square sail and oars.
The Sea Stallion is a 30-metre reconstruction of a Viking warship built near Dublin around 1042.
The Sea Stallion has a draught of 0.95 metres: it needs less than a metre of water.
Viking ships' shallow draught meant they could be used in shallow water and on rivers.
With their low keels, Viking warships could sail right onto a beach, and crews could drag them over land.
The Sea Stallion's estimated top speed under sail is 17 knots, and its 60 oars could keep it moving without wind.
In 2007-2008 the Sea Stallion sailed from Roskilde to Dublin and back as a test voyage.

title: Viking voyages
description: Vikings travelled east down Russian rivers to Kyiv and Constantinople, and west to Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland, where they were present in 1021.

facts.text: An eastern trade route along the rivers of Russia was controlled by Swedish Vikings.
The Viking Oleg, ruler of Novgorod, made Kyiv his capital around 882, founding the state of Kyivan Rus.
Rus merchants took convoys down the Dnieper River to Constantinople, hauling their ships overland around its rapids.
Norse settlers, most of them from Norway, settled Iceland in about 870-930.
About 985 Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, founded the first European settlement on Greenland, a name chosen to attract settlers.
About 1000, Erik's son Leif Erikson reached North America, and according to the sagas called part of it Vinland.
L'Anse aux Meadows, at Newfoundland's northern tip, is the first known evidence of Europeans in the Americas: a Norse timber-and-sod camp.
Wood cut with metal tools at L'Anse aux Meadows was felled in 1021, the first secure date for Europeans in the Americas (Kuitems, 2021).
The dating used a radiocarbon spike left in tree rings by a cosmic-ray event in 993; wood from three different trees gave the same year.
Metal tools like those that cut the wood were not made by the area's Indigenous inhabitants at the time.
Vikings crossed the Atlantic to the Americas centuries before Columbus.

title: Alfred defends Wessex
description: Alfred of Wessex survived the Viking onslaught of 878, won at Edington, agreed a border with the Danelaw and defended his kingdom with burhs, ships and learning.

facts.text: A great Danish army arrived in England in 865.
Alfred was king of Wessex from 871 to 899.
In early 878 the Danes seized Chippenham, and the West Saxons submitted, all except Alfred, who withdrew to the Somerset marshes.
The tale that Alfred, hiding in the marshes, let a peasant woman's cakes burn is a legend, first written down long after his death.
In May 878 Alfred defeated the Danes at Edington, and their leader Guthrum was baptized with Alfred as his godfather.
In 886 Alfred and the Danes agreed a frontier along Watling Street; the Danish-ruled north and east became the Danelaw, "Danes' law".
Alfred built fortified towns called burhs, so that no part of Wessex was more than 20 miles from one.
Alfred had a navy of fast new ships built, and Wessex was never again in such danger.
Alfred had Latin books translated into English and took part in the translating himself.
Alfred is the only English monarch known as "the Great".

title: The Normans
description: The Normans were Vikings who settled in northern France after Rollo's 911 treaty, took up French language and Christianity, and later won lands in England and southern Italy.

facts.text: Viking raids battered the Frankish coasts in the 9th century, and by about 900 Vikings had a permanent base in the Seine valley.
In 911 King Charles III the Simple granted Rollo the land around Rouen and the mouth of the Seine, by the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte.
In return, Rollo stopped his raiding, became a Christian and swore loyalty to Charles.
The settlers were called Nortmanni, "Northmen", which gave the words Norman and Normandy.
Rollo's Scandinavian settlers came in large numbers and adopted the French language, customs and religion.
Norman adventurers also won lands in southern Italy and Sicily, where Roger II became king of Sicily in 1130.

description: In 1066 Harold beat a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, then lost to William of Normandy at Hastings; how Harold died is debated.

facts.text: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066, and Harold Godwinson was crowned king.
William, duke of Normandy, claimed Edward had promised him the throne.
Harald Hardrada, king of Norway, another claimant, invaded the north with Harold's brother Tostig.
On 25 September 1066 Harold defeated the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge, near York; Hardrada and Tostig were both killed.
The Viking Age is traditionally said to have ended in 1066, with the battle of Stamford Bridge.
On 28 September 1066 William's invasion fleet landed at Pevensey, on the Sussex coast, and Harold marched south to meet it.
At the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066 the armies fought all day; Harold was killed late in the afternoon, and the English fled.
How Harold died is debated: the Tapestry's arrow was added in 19th-century repairs, and the nearest accounts suggest knights cut him down.
The Bayeux Tapestry is really an embroidery, in wool on linen, about 68 metres long.
William was crowned king of England in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

title: The Domesday Book
description: In 1086 William's commissioners surveyed who held England's land and what it was worth, for tax and defence; the record became Domesday Book.

facts.text: William ordered the survey at Christmas 1085, and it was carried out the following year, 1086.
William ordered it over problems in raising tax and organising defence, and because he did not know who held what land, or its worth.
Commissioners asked who held each manor under King Edward and now, how many plough teams and mills, and its worth in 1066 and now.
Domesday records how landholding had changed since the Norman Conquest of 1066.
A writer of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle complained that not one ox, cow or pig was left out of William's record.
Domesday Book mentions more than 13,000 places, most of which still exist; London and Winchester were left out.
First called the description of England, by the mid-12th century it was Domesday, after the Day of Judgement: a record with no appeal.
Domesday Book is kept at The National Archives.

title: From Northmen to Normans
description: Charlemagne built defences against the Northmen, but Vikings raided and settled anyway, and a Viking leader's descendant, William, conquered England.

facts.text: William the Conqueror was the great-great-great-grandson of the Viking leader Rollo.
Einhard wrote that Charlemagne built a fleet against the Northmen and posted guards at harbours and river mouths, as they raided the coasts.

title: Lords, vassals and fiefs
description: A lord granted a vassal a fief, usually land, in return for service; the bond was made by homage and fealty.

facts.text: A fief was a piece of property, usually land, that a vassal held from a lord in return for service, which could include military duties.
Vassals owed their lords military service, counsel and financial support; lords were expected to protect and respect their vassals.
Because a knight's armour and heavy horse were expensive to buy and maintain, the king in England granted land in return for knight service.
In the ceremony of homage a vassal became his lord's “man”; the word comes from Latin homo, “man”.
Vassals also swore fealty, a sworn promise of fidelity to their lord.

title: Feudalism: a debated label
description: Feudalism is a label coined centuries later; historians such as Brown and Reynolds showed the tidy pyramid is a simplification.

facts.text: Feudalism and feudal system are labels invented long after the Middle Ages: feudal system by the early 17th century, feudalism in English by the late 18th.
The tidy feudal pyramid is a simplification: relations between kings, lords, knights and peasants differed widely across medieval Europe.
In 1974 historian Elizabeth A. R. Brown's article “The Tyranny of a Construct” argued that feudalism has no agreed definition and is misleading.
In her 1994 book Fiefs and Vassals, Susan Reynolds argued that fief and vassal had no precise technical meaning until lawyers defined them in the late 12th century.
Since Brown and Reynolds, many medieval historians avoid the term feudalism.

title: What a serf was
description: A serf was bound to a hereditary plot and to his lord's will: not a slave, but not free to leave, marry or change work without permission.

facts.text: A medieval serf was bound to a hereditary plot of land and to the will of his lord.
Unlike serfs, slaves were bought and sold without reference to a plot of land.
A serf could not permanently leave his holding or village, marry, or change his occupation without his lord's permission.
A serf could gain freedom only by being formally freed by the lord (manumission or enfranchisement) or by escaping.

title: What peasants owed the manor
description: Villeins paid for their holdings with week-work on the lord's demesne, produce, and fees such as merchet and heriot.

facts.text: The demesne was the part of a manor the lord kept for his own use, and serfs supplied the labour to work it.
Week by week a villein had to plough the lord's demesne with his own plough and oxen, then harrow, reap, thresh and carry the crops: a duty called week-work.
A villein's holding included a dwelling, a number of acre strips in the fields and a share of the meadow.
A villein paid for his holding in money, in labour and in produce.
A substantial proportion of the grain a serf grew on his holding had to be given to his lord.
A serf had to use his lord's grain mill.
Merchet was a fee a villein paid his lord for permission to marry off his daughter.
When a villein died, his lord took a death duty called a heriot, usually the best beast.

title: What a castle was for
description: A castle was a lord's or king's fortified home, used to control the land around it.

facts.text: A castle was a medieval stronghold, generally the residence of the king or lord of the territory in which it stood.
Castles developed rapidly in western Europe from the 9th century.
Castles were something new in England after the Norman Conquest of 1066; they housed Norman nobles and their families, knights and soldiers.
Castles helped the Normans subdue the English and control the land they had conquered.

title: Motte and bailey
description: Early castles were earth mounds topped by timber towers beside a fenced yard, quick to build with forced labour.

facts.text: A motte was an artificial mound of earth and stone, shaped like an upside-down pudding bowl, topped by a timber tower.
The bailey was the fenced enclosure beside the motte, holding domestic buildings and animal pens.
Motte-and-bailey castles were quick to build, and could be raised by unskilled forced labourers using basic materials.
The timber towers on mottes were often prefabricated off-site, then put up like enormous flat-pack furniture.

title: Stone keeps
description: Stone replaced timber; the keep was the castle's strongest point.

facts.text: Stone castles eventually replaced earth-and-timber ones, because stone gave better defence and more status and prestige.
By the 12th century lords were building stone keeps, much easier to defend than wooden towers, some with walls six metres thick.
The keep was the strongest part of a castle's defences, holding a well, private apartments and provisions for a siege.

title: Walls, gates and murder holes
description: Moats, curtain walls, arrow loops, portcullises and murder holes made the way in the deadliest place.

facts.text: Castle defences included moats, crossed by drawbridges hinged at one end so they could be raised.
A curtain wall was a fortified wall around a castle, typically linking its towers together.
Arrow loops were narrow vertical slits in castle walls that let archers shoot out while staying behind the wall.
Gatehouses, the most vulnerable point of a castle, often became mini-castles in themselves.
A portcullis was a heavy wooden or iron grille that could be dropped in grooves to seal a castle entrance.
Murder holes were openings over a gate passage through which defenders dropped heavy stones, hot sand or boiling water on attackers.

title: Concentric castles
description: Rings of mutually supporting walls, as at Beaumaris, made attackers win again and again.

facts.text: The most powerful medieval stronghold was the concentric castle: two rings of mutually supporting towered walls, one inside the other.
At Beaumaris in Wales, Edward I and his architect James of St George built four concentric rings of defences, including a water-filled moat with its own dock.
Beaumaris Castle's outer walls alone had 300 arrow loops.
Lack of money and trouble in Scotland meant building at Beaumaris petered out by the 1320s, and the castle was never finished.

title: How to attack a castle
description: Ladders, siege towers, rams, mines and counterweight trebuchets.

facts.text: Climbing castle walls with ladders (escalade) rarely succeeded except by surprise or treachery.
Wheeled wooden siege towers could be fitted with drawbridges to drop onto a castle's wall.
Battering rams, protected by a wheeled wooden shed, were used to break down gates.
Miners dug under castle walls, propped the tunnel with timber, filled it with combustibles and set it alight so the wall above collapsed.
A counterweight trebuchet threw stones using a heavy counterweight on the short end of a pivoting beam.
Counterweight siege engines appeared in the 12th century.
Counterweight trebuchets could hurl objects weighing about 200 to 300 kg.

title: How sieges ended
description: Most sieges ended by treachery, starvation or disease; Rochester in 1215 fell to a pig-fat mine and then hunger.

facts.text: Medieval sieges were settled more often by treachery, starvation or disease than by breached walls.
Between October and December 1215 King John besieged Rochester Castle, held against him by rebels.
At Rochester in 1215 the royal army's siege engines bombarded the keep with stones while miners attacked its south-east turret.
King John's miners at Rochester burned the fat of 40 pigs too fat to eat to fire the timber props of their mine.
The fire brought down the south-east corner of Rochester's keep, and the rebels retreated to the northern half of the keep.
Starvation soon forced the rebels at Rochester to surrender.

title: Page and squire
description: A future knight served as a page from about 7, then as a squire learning arms and courtly skills.

facts.text: A youth destined for knighthood might serve as a page from the age of about 7.
At about 12 a future knight would join the household of his father's lord for further training, where he might be called a damoiseau, “lordling”.
A squire was a young man of noble birth apprenticed in the duties of chivalry, who looked after a knight's armour and weapons.
A squire's training included hunting, music and dancing, and aimed to produce a worthy knight, a just master and a sensible manager of an estate.

title: Dubbing a knight
description: The accolade made a knight; equipment was costly, and many knights held fiefs as vassals.

facts.text: A new knight was dubbed with the accolade, a touch on the shoulder with the flat of a sword blade.
A new knight had to buy his own knightly equipment, a considerable expense.
In France some squires were noble youths waiting for, or putting off, the expensive dubbing.
Many knights were vassals holding lands as fiefs from the lords in whose armies they served.

title: From mail to plate
description: Mail of interlocking links gave way, from the late 13th century and fast after 1325, to full plate harness.

facts.text: Before plate, the standard metal armour in Europe was mail, a flexible mesh of interlocking iron links, worn over quilted garments.
A mail shirt, or hauberk, contained thousands of links and was expensive and time-consuming to make.
Mail was flexible and protected well against sword cuts, but was less effective against piercing and crushing blows such as arrows and maces.
Plate armour emerged in Europe in the late 13th century.
Between 1325 and 1340 a revolution in European armour replaced or reinforced mail with plates of iron or steel.
Through the 14th century plate defences spread to the rest of the body, until the complete suit of plate, the harness, was developed.
Rigid steel plates deflected glancing blows; a weapon could only penetrate plate if it struck directly and with great force.

title: How heavy armour really was
description: Field armour weighed about 20 to 25 kg, spread over the body; knights were never hoisted by cranes.

facts.text: Films have shown knights winched onto their horses by cranes, for example the 1944 Henry V; the idea has no medieval basis.
A complete suit of field armour usually weighed about 20 to 25 kg (45 to 55 lb).
The weight of plate armour was distributed over the whole body, so a man in armour stayed remarkably agile.
Even a suddenly unhorsed knight in armour could quickly get up again, ready for combat.
Modern tests show a man in properly fitted armour can mount and dismount a horse, lie on the ground and get up again.

title: The chivalric ideal
description: Chivalry first meant mounted knights and became an ideal of honour, loyalty, faith and protecting the weak.

facts.text: In medieval Europe the word chivalry first meant knights, fully armed and mounted fighting men; it later came to mean courtesy.
Chivalry as honourable and courteous conduct expected of a knight was perhaps at its height in the 12th and 13th centuries.
The Christian ideal of chivalry involved respect for the Church, protection of the poor and weak, loyalty to one's superiors, and personal honour.

title: Chivalry in practice
description: In practice mercy was for ransomable nobles, and historians like Kaeuper see chivalry as part of the problem of violence.

facts.text: A captured enemy knight might be spared if it paid in land, gold or booty, not for altruistic reasons; knights fought pragmatically.
Ransoms and plunder from war could bring great profits.
Chivalry centred on the noble warrior on horseback; its protections did not extend to peasants, who were often slaughtered when in the way.
In 1999 historian Richard Kaeuper argued that chivalry was part of the problem of violence in medieval Europe, not merely its solution.
In chivalric writing, prowess, skill at violent deeds, became almost a one-word definition of chivalry.
The Church tried to regulate the violence of knights, and chivalry as a concept grew partly out of those efforts.

title: Why heraldry began
description: Heraldry took shape in the 12th century to tell armoured men apart.

facts.text: In 1127 King Henry I of England hung a blue shield with golden lions around the neck of Geoffrey of Anjou, his future son-in-law.
As body armour became all-enveloping, a way to tell men in full armour apart grew more important, which sped the spread of heraldry.
European heraldry took shape in the 12th century.
Heralds can be identified in descriptions of tournaments from about 1170.

title: Reading a coat of arms
description: Coats of arms used set metals and colours, a rule of contrast, and became hereditary.

facts.text: The term coat of arms comes from the surcoat, a cloth tunic worn over armour that displayed the bearer's arms.
Heraldry's metals are gold (or) and silver (argent); its colours include red (gules), blue (azure), green (vert), purple (purpure) and black (sable).
Heraldry follows a rule of contrast, generally avoiding colour on colour and metal on metal, so that designs stay visible.
Heraldic arms tended to become hereditary, passed down through families.

title: Pray, fight, work
description: Early 11th-century bishops described society as three orders: those who pray, fight and work.

facts.text: In the early 11th century, bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society as three orders: those who pray, those who fight and those who work.

title: The parish church in daily life
description: The parish church was normally the only place to receive the sacraments and be buried, and councils like Lateran IV (1215) set yearly duties for every believer.

facts.text: The medieval parish church was often the largest building in a parish, and usually the only one that mattered to all parishioners regardless of age or wealth.
Apart from extreme unction (the last anointing), the medieval parish church was normally the only place parishioners could receive the sacraments, and it was where they were buried.
In the 12th century Peter Lombard, whose Sentences became the standard theological text of the Middle Ages, taught that there are seven sacraments.
The seven sacraments include baptism, the Eucharist and marriage, along with confirmation, penance, anointing of the sick and holy orders.
The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, called by Pope Innocent III, drew more than 400 bishops and 800 abbots and priors.
The Fourth Lateran Council obliged Catholics to confess at least once a year and to receive Communion during Lent.

title: The tithe
description: Believers owed the Church a tithe, a tenth of their income, which paid clergy, churches, the poor and even cathedrals.

facts.text: A tithe was a tenth of a person's income given for religious purposes, paid in money or its equivalent in crops and farm animals.
Tithes supported the clergy, maintained churches and helped the poor.
Tithes were required by church law from the 6th century and enforced in Europe by kings' secular law from the 8th century.
Tithes were a prime source of money for building many of Europe's great cathedrals.

title: The Investiture Controversy
description: Popes and kings fought over who installed bishops; Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV, and the Concordat of Worms (1122) split the difference.

facts.text: In lay investiture a king handed a new bishop a crosier and ring, saying "receive the church"; they stood for both the spiritual office and its lands and property.
In 1075 Pope Gregory VII issued the Dictatus papae, asserting papal primacy, including that a pope could depose emperors.
In January 1076 the German king Henry IV and his bishops renounced obedience to Pope Gregory VII and called on him to step down.
In February 1076 Gregory VII deposed and excommunicated Henry IV, the first pope to depose a crowned ruler.
Excommunication shut a person out of the communion of believers, the rites or sacraments of the church and the rights of church membership.
In the Concordat of Worms (1122), Henry V gave up investing bishops with ring and crosier and accepted their free election, but kept the right to invest them with their lands.

title: Canossa, 1077
description: Excommunicated, Henry IV waited three days as a penitent at Canossa in January 1077 before Gregory VII absolved him.

facts.text: In January 1077 Henry IV went to Canossa as a penitent and, after waiting three days, was absolved by Gregory VII on January 28.
Henry IV crossed the Alps in winter and, according to tradition, stood barefoot in the snow for three days before the castle at Canossa.
During Prussia's Kulturkampf against Catholic influence, Otto von Bismarck declared "We are not going to Canossa".

title: Gothic engineering
description: Rib vaults, pointed arches and flying buttresses let Gothic builders go taller and open walls into windows, sometimes past the limit, as at Beauvais.

facts.text: In a rib vault, stone ribs carry the vaulted ceiling; together with the pointed arch, it let Gothic builders cover broader, taller and more complicated buildings.
A flying buttress is a half arch that carries the thrust of a vault across an aisle to an outer pier, letting builders go taller and open the walls into larger windows.
The east end of the abbey church of Saint-Denis, rebuilt about 1135 to 1144 under Abbot Suger, is traditionally the first Gothic building.
The choir of Beauvais Cathedral has the tallest Gothic stone vault in the world.
In November 1284 Beauvais's flying buttresses twisted and broke and the choir vault collapsed, probably triggered by a storm; rebuilding took until about 1340.

title: How cathedrals were built
description: Master masons, templates, shipped stone and treadwheel cranes built cathedrals over decades or centuries, as at Canterbury and Cologne.

facts.text: Work on Cologne Cathedral began in 1248, stalled for centuries after the 1500s, and finally ended in 1880, 632 years later.
On a cathedral site the master mason provided templates for the shaped stones and put a master craftsman in charge of each area of work.
Canterbury Cathedral's builders brought stone by boat from France, easier than hauling it overland on poor roads.
Builders reached high work on scaffolding and lifted stones with cranes and pulleys, including a treadwheel: a "hamster wheel" big enough for two men.

title: Pilgrimage and its shrines
description: Medieval Christians made pilgrimages for penance, cures, vows and salvation, to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and other shrines.

facts.text: Medieval Christians went on pilgrimage to seek salvation, fulfil vows, do penance or hope for miraculous cures.
At Jerusalem and Rome, medieval pilgrims could gain indulgences, which the Church taught remitted the penalty of sin.
Santiago de Compostela in Spain was the third most important pilgrimage destination after Jerusalem and Rome; the apostle James's body was believed to have been brought there.
The scallop shell was the emblem of St James and Santiago de Compostela, and pilgrims wore badges on their necks, clothes or bags.
Many pilgrims believed a saint's power passed into a souvenir that touched the shrine, and some buried souvenirs in house foundations for protection.

title: Becket and Canterbury
description: Thomas Becket's murder in 1170 made Canterbury England's great shrine, the goal of Chaucer's pilgrims.

facts.text: Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral by four knights on December 29, 1170.
Becket was made a saint in 1173.
A whole industry grew up at Canterbury around the large numbers of pilgrims visiting Becket's shrine.
Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (1387-1400) follows 30 pilgrims from the Tabard Inn in Southwark to Becket's shrine, telling stories in a contest.

title: The Divine Office
description: Monks and nuns sang a daily cycle of services at set hours, from matins in the night to compline.

facts.text: The Divine Office was a daily round of psalms, hymns, prayers and readings, said or sung at set hours.
Its hours were matins (the longest, originally at night), lauds and vespers (morning and evening), prime (early morning), terce, sext and none (mid-morning, noon, mid-afternoon) and compline (night).

title: The cloister
description: The cloister, a square of covered walkways, linked the church, refectory, chapter house and dormitory and was used for study, exercise and burial.

facts.text: A cloister was a square enclosure ringed by covered walkways; in Benedictine houses the church stood on one side, the refectory opposite, the chapter house on the east and the dormitory upstairs.
In the cloister younger members were educated and elders studied; it was also used for exercise, and its walks and centre were customary burial places.

title: Nuns and convents
description: Nuns lived by the Benedictine pattern under an abbess, in mostly small, enclosed houses.

facts.text: A medieval English nun's day had three parts: singing eight services, devotional reading and manual labour.
An abbess was the superior of a community of nuns following the Benedictine Rule, and abbesses occasionally ruled double monasteries of monks and nuns.
Strict rules of enclosure forbade medieval nuns to leave their monastery for work in the wider community.
Most English nunneries after the Norman Conquest were small and poor; only a minority had more than a dozen or so nuns.

title: Hildegard of Bingen
description: Hildegard (born 1098), a German abbess, recorded visions, wrote on medicine, preached and corresponded with popes and an emperor.

facts.text: Hildegard of Bingen, born in 1098, was a German abbess, visionary and composer.
Hildegard was educated by Jutta at the Benedictine cloister of Disibodenberg, took the habit at 15 and succeeded Jutta as prioress in 1136.
About 1147 Hildegard left Disibodenberg with several nuns to found a new convent at Rupertsberg, near Bingen.
At 43 Hildegard consulted her confessor about her visions; her Scivias (1141-52) describes 26 of them.
Hildegard travelled widely in Germany, preaching to large crowds about her visions.
At Rupertsberg Hildegard cared for the sick and wrote two medical works: Causes and Cures, on theory, and Physica, on remedies.
About 390 of Hildegard's letters survive, to correspondents including popes, an emperor, kings and queens, clergy and lay people.
In 2012 Hildegard was canonized and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church.

title: Hildegard's music
description: Hildegard composed songs and the Ordo virtutum, the earliest known morality play, in which only the Devil does not sing.

facts.text: Hildegard collected 77 of her poems, each set to music she composed, in the Symphonia.
Hildegard's Ordo virtutum (Play of the Virtues) is the earliest known morality play; its 17 Virtues are sung by female soloists.
In the Ordo virtutum the Devil speaks rather than sings, because Hildegard believed the Devil had no divine harmony.

title: The first universities
description: Universities began as guilds of students and masters: Bologna late in the 11th century, then Paris and Oxford.

facts.text: The first universities were corporations of students and masters, which received charters from popes, emperors and kings.
The first true university in the West grew up at Bologna late in the 11th century and became a leading school of canon and civil law.
At Bologna, scholars of the same nationality formed guilds to secure protections they could not claim as citizens.
In 1158 Emperor Frederick I granted privileges to the scholars of Bologna, later extended to all Italian universities.
The University of Paris, northern Europe's first, was founded between 1150 and 1170 and became known for theology; Oxford was well established by the end of the 12th century.
Medieval universities grew from studia generalia, recognized places of study open to students from all parts of Europe.

title: A round Earth in the classroom
description: Medieval universities taught a spherical Earth from Sacrobosco's Sphere; the flat-Earth Middle Ages is a 19th-century myth.

facts.text: Johannes de Sacrobosco, who taught at Paris, wrote The Sphere about 1230; it became the most popular university textbook on astronomy.
Sacrobosco's Sphere argued at length that the Earth is a sphere.
The Sphere circulated in handwritten copies for 240 years and was then printed again and again from 1476.
Medieval scholars knew the Earth is a sphere; the idea that medieval people thought it flat is a myth spread by 19th-century writers.

title: The excommunications of 1054
description: In 1054 a papal legate and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, the traditional date of the East-West split; the sentences were lifted in 1965.

facts.text: On July 16, 1054, the papal legate Cardinal Humbert entered Hagia Sophia and excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius and his clergy.
Pope Leo IX, who had sent the legates, had died before Humbert's excommunication.
In response, Cerularius convened a synod that excommunicated the pope's legates.
The mutual excommunications of 1054 became a watershed in church history, the traditional date of the split between the Latin and Orthodox churches.
The excommunications were not lifted until 1965, when Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I held simultaneous ceremonies revoking them.
The excommunications of 1054 stood for 911 years, until they were revoked in 1965.

title: Why East and West drifted apart
description: Disputes over papal authority, the Creed, celibacy and bread widened a gap that grew from the 5th to the 11th century.

facts.text: Relations between the Byzantine and Roman churches were a growing estrangement from the 5th to the 11th century.

The East never accepted Rome's growing claim to preeminence, objected that Rome added "and the Son" to the Creed without consulting it, and resented Roman rules on clerical celibacy and unleavened bread.

title: Heresy and the Cathars
description: Heresy was belief rejected by church authorities; the dualist Cathars were the best-known medieval example.

facts.text: Heresy is a doctrine rejected as false by church authorities.
The Cathars believed in two principles, one good and one evil, and held that the material world is evil.
Catharism spread in western Europe in the 12th and 13th centuries; its leaders, the perfect, were set apart by a ceremony called the consolamentum.
Under Pope Innocent III, a crusade against the Cathars began in 1209.

title: The medieval inquisition
description: Papal inquisitors from 1227 tried suspected heretics; most received penances or prison, and those who refused to recant were burned.

facts.text: From 1227 Pope Gregory IX appointed the first inquisitors to investigate heresy; many were Dominican and Franciscan friars.
An inquisitor announced a period of grace when those who confessed received light penances; suspects were not normally told the charges or who had accused them.
In 1252 Pope Innocent IV allowed inquisitors to have stubborn suspects tortured by lay officials.
Convicted heretics faced penitential pilgrimages, yellow crosses sewn on their clothes or prison; those who refused to recant were handed to secular authorities and burned.
At Verona in 1278, more than 150 Cathars were burned together.
Burnings were usually not numerous, because the inquisitors' chief aim was to reconcile heretics to the Church.
Film made the Toulouse inquisitor Bernard Gui a byword for cruelty, but his records show that of hundreds he sentenced, a few dozen were burned.

title: The Church and the two powers
description: Medieval thinkers divided Christendom into clergy and rulers, but the Church also held land, armies and learning.

facts.text: Medieval Christendom was thought to consist of two groups, the sacerdotium (clergy) and the imperium (secular rulers), with the pope supreme in the first and the emperor in the second.
The medieval Church owned cities and armies and often tried to regulate affairs of state.
Intellectual life in medieval Europe was dominated by the Roman Catholic Church.

title: Urban II's call of 1095
description: A Byzantine appeal for help against the Turks led Pope Urban II to call Western knights east at Clermont in 1095, offering the remission of penance for sin.

facts.text: Envoys of the Byzantine emperor Alexius I Comnenus asked Pope Urban II for help against the Seljuk Turks.
At the Council of Clermont, in France, in November 1095, Pope Urban II urged Western knights to go east and rescue the Holy Land from the Turks.
Urban II's exact words at Clermont are unknown: the only surviving accounts of his speech were written years later.
Urban's speech was answered with cries of "God wills it", and those who agreed to go were to wear a cross.
The word crusade comes, through French and Spanish, from Latin crux, "cross".
Urban's council granted a plenary indulgence, the remission of all penance for sin, to those who went to aid the Christians of the East.
Crusaders believed that fighting what they saw as a holy war was a way to win redemption and make up for their sins.

title: The Rhineland massacres of 1096
description: In May 1096 crusader bands attacked the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, a turning point in Jewish-Christian relations.

facts.text: In May 1096, crusader bands attacked the Jewish communities of Rhineland towns including Speyer, Worms and Mainz.
Crusaders left many Rhineland Jews only a choice between baptism and death, and some chose death.
At Mainz the Jews sheltered in the bishop's castle, but he fled before the attack, and more than 1,000 Jews were killed.
The 1096 massacres are traditionally seen as a turning point in Jewish-Christian relations and a pivotal moment in the history of antisemitism.

title: The First Crusade
description: The First Crusade reached a divided Muslim Near East, took Antioch in 1098 and stormed Fatimid-held Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, killing many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

facts.text: The People's Crusade, stirred up by the preacher Peter the Hermit, was ambushed and all but annihilated by the Turks in Anatolia in 1096.
The main crusader armies captured Antioch in June 1098, after a long siege.
The crusaders faced divided enemies: the Seljuk empire never held together as a unit, and Shi'i Fatimid Egypt and Sunni Baghdad were rivals.
The Fatimids of Egypt had taken Jerusalem in August 1098, so the crusaders' final drive was against them, not the Seljuk Turks.
On 15 July 1099 the crusaders stormed Jerusalem, and many of its Muslim and Jewish men, women and children were killed in the slaughter that followed.
Jerusalem's Jews fought beside their Muslim neighbors in 1099, then sheltered in synagogues that the attackers set on fire.
Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen to govern Jerusalem and took the modest title Defender of the Holy Sepulchre.

title: The crusader states
description: The crusaders set up four states, called Outremer, ruled by a Christian minority; Bohemond kept Antioch despite his oath to Byzantium, and Edessa's fall in 1144 led to the failed Second Crusade.

facts.text: After the First Crusade four crusader states were set up: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli.
Europeans called the crusader states Outremer, French for "overseas".
Godfrey's brother Baldwin first became ruler of Edessa, then took the title of king of Jerusalem in November 1100 after Godfrey died.
Emperor Alexius made each crusade leader swear to restore to him any conquered land that had belonged to his empire before the Turkish invasions.
Bohemond, who had led the capture of Antioch, ignored his oath and kept the city for himself instead of returning it to the emperor.
The crusader states were feudal lands ruled by a Christian minority over diverse local peoples, including Muslims and many Christian groups.
In 1144 the Muslim ruler Zengi captured Edessa, the northernmost and weakest crusader state, and its loss led to the Second Crusade.
The Second Crusade, led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany, failed at Damascus in 1148, leaving the crusader states on the defensive.

title: Saladin
description: Saladin, a Kurdish commander who became ruler of Egypt and Syria, destroyed the crusader army at Hattin and took Jerusalem by ransomed surrender in 1187; the West later made him a legend.

facts.text: Saladin was born in 1137 or 1138 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq, into a prominent Kurdish family.
In 1169, at the age of 31, Saladin became vizier of Egypt.
In 1171 Saladin abolished the Shi'i Fatimid caliphate and returned Egypt to Sunni Islam.
From 1174 to 1186 Saladin worked to unite Syria, northern Mesopotamia, Palestine and Egypt under his rule.
Saladin was intensely devoted to the idea of jihad, holy war, against the crusaders.
On 4 July 1187, at Hattin in northern Palestine, Saladin trapped and destroyed an exhausted, thirst-stricken crusader army.
After Hattin, Saladin spared King Guy and most of the lords but ordered the execution of almost all captured Templars and Hospitallers.
Jerusalem surrendered to Saladin on 2 October 1187, after 88 years in the hands of the Franks.
Saladin had planned to avenge the 1099 slaughter by killing Jerusalem's Christians, but agreed to let the inhabitants buy their freedom.
Several thousand of Jerusalem's people were apparently not ransomed in 1187 and were probably sold into slavery.
Western chroniclers praised Saladin as a gallant, chivalrous enemy, and Western novels and films celebrated his generosity for centuries.
Saladin died in Damascus in March 1193, leaving too little money to pay for his grave.

title: Richard I and the Third Crusade
description: Richard I took Acre and won at Arsuf in the Third Crusade (1189-1192) but never retook Jerusalem; he and Saladin agreed a truce in 1192 without ever meeting.

facts.text: Richard I and Saladin, the famous rivals of the Third Crusade, never actually met.
Saladin's victory at Hattin prompted Europe to launch the Third Crusade, which lasted from 1189 to 1192.
Emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned crossing a river in 1190, on his way to the Third Crusade.
On his way east, Richard conquered Cyprus, which became a vital source of supplies for the crusade.
Acre surrendered to the crusaders in July 1191, and in August Philip II of France went home.
When Saladin failed to pay an agreed ransom, Richard had all 2,700 members of Acre's Muslim garrison executed in view of Saladin's army.
Richard won at Arsuf in September 1191 and twice led his army to within a few miles of Jerusalem, but both times retreated and never retook the city.
Richard kept in constant contact with Saladin and his brother al-Adil, and the two sides showed considerable mutual respect.
In September 1192 Richard and Saladin agreed a three-year truce: the coast from Jaffa north stayed Christian, and pilgrims had free access to the holy places.
Sailing home, Richard was captured by Duke Leopold of Austria, handed to Emperor Henry VI, and freed in 1194 for a ransom of 150,000 marks.
Richard, king of England from 1189 to 1199, spent little time in England, and recent historians have judged him less kindly than his contemporaries did.

title: The Knights Templar
description: The Templars, founded around 1120 to protect pilgrims, were fighting monks and bankers; after Acre fell, Philip IV had them arrested in 1307 on baseless charges and the pope suppressed the order in 1312.

facts.text: In late 1119 or early 1120, eight or nine French knights led by Hugh de Payns vowed to protect pilgrims traveling to the Holy Land.
King Baldwin II of Jerusalem gave the knights quarters in the area of the former Temple of Solomon, which gave them their name.
Within about ten years of its founding, the Church formally approved the Templar order at the Council of Troyes (dated 1128 or 1129).
Templars swore vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, and the knights wore a white surcoat marked with a red cross.
The Templars' military strength made them ideal bankers, to kings as well as to pilgrims.
After Acre fell in 1291 the Templars lost much of their reason for being, while their wealth, lands in Europe and power bred resentment.
On 13 October 1307, Philip IV of France, chronically short of money, had every Templar in France arrested.
The Templars were accused of heresy and idol worship, many confessed under torture, and the charges are now recognized as baseless.
Pope Clement V suppressed the Templars in 1312 and gave their property to the Hospitallers; the last grand master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in 1314.

title: The Fourth Crusade and 1204
description: In debt to Venice and lured by an exiled prince, the Fourth Crusade attacked Christian Zara and in April 1204 sacked Constantinople, setting up a Latin empire until 1261.

facts.text: Pope Innocent III called a new crusade in 1198.
The crusaders contracted with Venice for transport costing 85,000 marks, but in 1202 only about a third of the expected army arrived, and they could not pay.
To settle their debt to Venice, the crusaders attacked and took the Christian city of Zara (Zadar) in November 1202.
An exiled Byzantine prince, Alexius, promised the crusaders a huge payment, the Byzantine church's submission to Rome and help on crusade if they put him on the throne.
On 12 April 1204 the crusaders broke into Constantinople from the water, with men climbing from ships' masts across catwalks onto the walls.
For three days in April 1204 the crusaders pillaged Constantinople at will, defiling and stealing from its holy places.
Hagia Sophia was looted during the sack of 1204 and served as a Roman Catholic cathedral until 1261.
The four bronze horses of St Mark's in Venice were brought from Constantinople at the time of the Fourth Crusade.
When Pope Innocent III heard how the crusaders had behaved, he was filled with shame and rebuked them.
The crusaders made Baldwin of Flanders emperor of a new Latin empire, and in 1261 Michael VIII Palaeologus retook a much diminished Constantinople.

title: The Reconquista
description: Over nearly eight centuries, Christian kingdoms took back the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule, from Covadonga around 718 to Granada in 1492.

facts.text: The Reconquista was a series of campaigns by Christian states to retake the Iberian Peninsula from the Muslims, who had occupied most of it in the early 8th century.
The traditional start of the Reconquista is the Battle of Covadonga, around 718, when Christians in Asturias, in northern Spain, first held off Muslim forces.
In 1085 King Alfonso VI captured Toledo.
In 1212, at Las Navas de Tolosa, an alliance of Christian kingdoms defeated the Almohads, removing the last serious Muslim threat to Christian dominance.
Ferdinand III of Castile conquered Cordoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248.

Granada, seat of the last Moorish kingdom in Spain and home of the Alhambra, fell to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic Monarchs, in January 1492, nearly 800 years after the Muslim conquest began in 711.
The Reconquista began as political expansion; popes backed it by the 11th century, but it became explicitly religious only after Muslim power in Spain was broken.
Over the centuries, the Christian and Muslim peoples of Spain became tightly bound together, culturally and economically.

title: What the Crusades changed
description: After Acre fell in 1291, the Crusades left richer Italian trading cities, embittered Greeks, long memories among Jews and Muslims, and less influence on learning than once claimed.

facts.text: In 1291 the Mamluks took Acre, the last crusader stronghold on the mainland, and destroyed it and the castles along the coast.
Italian cities gained quarters in the crusader states, extended their trade with the Muslim world and set up trading posts, some lasting long after 1291.
Crusading expanded trade between Europe and the Muslim world, bringing new goods and tastes to Europeans.
The Crusades, especially the Fourth, so embittered the Greeks that any real reunion of the Eastern and Western churches became out of the question.
Muslim writers of the time called the crusaders Franks and saw them as cruel invaders.
Unlike Sicily and Spain, the crusader states do not seem to have been a route for Arabic science and philosophy to reach the West.
Historians now see the Crusades as one significant factor in Europe's development, not its single driving force.

title: The crusading era at a glance
description: From 1095 to 1291 the Crusades filled almost two centuries of the high Middle Ages and drew Rome's three heirs, the Latin West, Byzantium and the Islamic world, into one story.

facts.text: From Urban II's call in 1095 to the fall of Acre in 1291, crusading in the Holy Land lasted almost two centuries.
The Crusades of 1095 to 1291 fall in the high Middle Ages, between the early period (to about 1000) and the late period (from about 1300).
The First Crusade began when the Byzantine emperor asked the pope in the West for help against Muslim Turks, drawing all three of Rome's heirs into one conflict.

title: Why towns grew after 1000
description: Once raids ended, western European towns revived: Europe's population nearly doubled between 1000 and 1340, and new walled towns were founded.

facts.text: In western Europe, urban communities grew steadily again only after the attacks by Magyars, Vikings and Saracens had stopped.
Europe's population is estimated to have risen from about 38.5 million in 1000 to about 73.5 million in 1340, nearly doubling.
In the 10th and 11th centuries new towns were founded and existing ones grew in area and population; they were usually enclosed within a wall.

title: Charters and "city air"
description: Self-governing towns (communes) held charters from bishops, counts or kings, and many offered freedom to settlers who stayed a year and a day.

facts.text: A medieval commune was a self-governing town whose citizens swore an oath of mutual help; it was originally chartered by a bishop, count or king.
Emperor Henry V affirmed the principle "Stadtluft macht frei" ("city air brings freedom") in charters for the towns of Speyer and Worms.
New towns founded on lords' lands offered freedom and land to settlers who lived there for more than a year and a day.
Henry V was Holy Roman emperor from 1111 to 1125.

title: Weekly markets
description: An English market met once a week on a set day and place, by royal charter, and from 1200 only if it did not harm its neighbours.

facts.text: In medieval England and Wales a market was held once a week, on a set day and in a set place.
In medieval England a royal charter gave a town, village, monastery or other religious house the right to hold a regular market.
From 1200, English royal grants allowed a new market or fair only if it did not harm neighbouring markets or fairs.

title: Fairs and the Champagne fairs
description: Fairs met once a year on saints' days; the great Champagne fairs linked northern cloth and Mediterranean spices, used credit, and fair courts settled disputes on the spot.

facts.text: A medieval fair was held once a year on a set date, usually a saint's feast day, and could last from one day to a week or more.
The Champagne fairs rotated among four towns, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes, and reached their peak in the 13th century.
At the Champagne fairs, protected by the count's privilege, northern cloth was exchanged for spices and dyes from Mediterranean lands.
Deals at the Champagne fairs often used letters of credit, laying groundwork for modern credit.
Piepowder courts, named from the French for "dusty feet", settled disputes at English fairs and markets quickly and on the spot.

title: What guilds did
description: Merchant and craft guilds grew up in busy towns; craft guilds held a local monopoly, set quality and prices, and had patron saints, chapels and charity.

facts.text: Merchant guilds grouped the merchants of a town; craft guilds grouped the artisans of one branch of industry or trade.
Craft guilds arose soon after merchant guilds, in expanding towns where an extensive division of labour was emerging.
Guilds held a monopoly of trade in their town or branch of industry, set standards for the quality of goods and worked to keep prices stable.
A guild often had a patron saint and kept a chapel in the parish church; guilds also did charitable work and built guildhalls.

title: Apprentice, journeyman, master
description: Guild members climbed from apprentice (five to nine years, living with the master) to journeyman (paid by the day) to master, by way of a masterpiece.

facts.text: Guild members were ranked as masters, journeymen and apprentices; apprentices, boys in late childhood or adolescence, boarded with the master's family for five to nine years.
The "journey" in journeyman originally meant a day's labour: journeymen worked for wages, often paid by the day.
A journeyman who proved his technical skill with a "masterpiece" might rise to become a master.

title: Food by rank
description: Bread quality, meat and drink all marked rank: fine wheat for lords, coarse loaves for servants, meat rarely for peasants, and fish on fast days.

facts.text: In a medieval castle, bakers made fine white wheat rolls for the lady's table and rough loaves of barley, oats or even peas and beans for servants.
At medieval feasts food was often served on slices of bread that caught the juices, and eaten with the fingers; forks did not appear on medieval tables.
Meat on the table was a sign of status; peasants ate it only rarely, mainly before winter, when livestock was culled so fewer animals had to be fed through winter.
Religious fasting banned meat on Fridays and many other days of the year, so fish took its place.
At medieval feasts, lower-ranking diners got coarser bread and second-quality ale, while wine was expensive because it was imported.

title: Spices as status
description: Spices were costly imports for the rich, used in strong sauces to show wealth; historians reject the myth that they hid rotten meat.

facts.text: Spices were costly imports, and lords served strong-tasting sauces made with expensive foreign spices to show off their wealth.
Historians reject the idea that spices hid rotten meat: spices cost far more than fresh meat, and salting and smoking preserved food better.

title: Cloth as a badge of rank
description: Wool clothed almost everyone, from cheap russet to costly scarlet; pointed shoes were a fashion whose mark shows in medieval bones.

facts.text: In 14th-century England wool was the most commonly bought fabric, from cheap russet and blanket to costly scarlet; linen came second.
Pointed shoes called poulaines were a late-medieval fashion; in 1463 King Edward IV limited their toe points in London to under two inches.
Cambridge researchers found bunions in 6% of people buried in the 11th to 13th centuries but 27% of those buried in the 14th and 15th, and linked the rise to pointed shoes.

title: Sumptuary laws
description: Laws such as England's of 1363 set what each rank could wear, to stop people dressing above their station, but proved hard to enforce.

facts.text: An English law of 1363 set what cloth people of each social rank could wear, from servants and craftsmen up to merchants and knights.
The 1363 law blamed the "outrageous and excessive apparel" of people dressing against their "estate and degree".
Under the 1363 law the lowest ranks could wear only blanket and russet, coarse wool cloth worth no more than 12 pence.
Sumptuary laws have proved difficult or impossible to enforce over the long term.

title: Water and wind power
description: Thousands of watermills ground England's grain by 1086; windmills, first known in Persia, appear in English records in the 1180s as timber post mills.

facts.text: In 1086 a royal survey recorded more than 5,000 water mills in England south of the Severn and Trent rivers.
Waterwheels were first used to grind grain and were later adapted to drive sawmills, bellows for forges and furnaces, trip-hammers and textile mills.
The earliest-known references to windmills come from Persia, in the years 644 and 915.
The earliest written references that clearly mention windmills in England date from the 1180s.
The earliest European windmills were timber post mills: the whole body, holding the millstones and gears, turned on a central post to face the wind.

title: The lord's mill
description: Lords claimed the right to grind all their tenants' grain and took a toll for it, which is why Abbot Samson destroyed a rival windmill in 1191.

facts.text: A lord could claim soke, or suit of mill: the right to grind at his mill all the grain used in his manor.
Millers were paid by toll, a share taken from each person's grain.
In 1191 Abbot Samson of Bury St Edmunds ordered the destruction of a windmill that Herbert the dean had built without his permission.
Samson told the dean the town's burgesses would take their grain to the new mill instead of his; the frightened dean had it pulled down himself.
Samson told the dean: "I give you as many thanks as if you had cut off both my feet."

title: The four humours
description: Medieval medicine held that blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile had to stay in balance; the theory came from Hippocrates and Galen and left words like sanguine.

facts.text: Medieval medicine held to the ancient theory of four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler) and black bile (melancholy).
In humoral theory the ideal person had a balanced mixture of the four humours, and illness came from an imbalance.
Hippocrates championed humoral theory, and Galen, Rome's leading medical authority in the 2nd century CE, made bloodletting prominent.
A person ruled by one humour was called sanguine (from Latin sanguis, blood), phlegmatic, choleric or melancholic.

title: Diagnosis and bloodletting
description: Physicians read urine for signs of imbalance and removed "excess" humours by bloodletting, often done by barber-surgeons; the practice was later discredited.

facts.text: Medieval physicians examined a patient's urine, its colour, consistency, clarity and sediment, for signs of imbalance in the four humours.
To cure illness, healers tried to remove the excess humour, for example by letting blood or applying leeches.
After a church edict of 1163 barred clergy from bloodletting, barber-surgeons took it up alongside shaving and pulling teeth, a legacy seen in the barber pole.
Bloodletting lost credibility in the 18th and 19th centuries, when studies showed it worked less well than its supporters claimed.

title: What medieval women did
description: Examples by class and region: Christine de Pizan wrote for a living in France, Margaret Paston ran and defended Norfolk estates, English brewsters and Paris silkwomen worked in trade.

facts.text: Christine de Pizan (1364 to about 1430), widowed after ten years of marriage, took up writing to support herself and her three children.
Christine de Pizan's Book of the City of Ladies (1405) told of women known for heroism and virtue, and she defended women against misogynist satire.
Margaret Paston (about 1421 to 1484), a Norfolk gentlewoman, left the largest collection of personal letters from medieval England, many to her husband while he was away.
While her husband was away, Margaret Paston managed the family's estates, defended their manor house against attackers and asked him for crossbows and armour.
Women brewed and sold most of the ale drunk in medieval England; after 1350 men slowly took over the trade.
In 13th- and 14th-century Paris the silk industry had some all-female guilds, and a few silkwomen did business with aristocrats and even the king.

title: Coverture and its limits
description: In England a married woman's legal existence was suspended under coverture, while a single woman could contract and sue in her own name.

facts.text: Under coverture, rooted in Norman custom, an English wife's legal existence was suspended: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name, though a single woman could.

title: Holy days and festivals
description: Free time followed the Church calendar ("holiday" means holy day); at York the craft guilds staged a 48-play cycle on Corpus Christi.

facts.text: The word holiday comes from Old English haligdæg, "holy day", a day set apart for religious observance; by the 14th century it could also mean a day off work.
The York plays, dating from the 14th century, were a cycle of 48 plays performed by the city's craft guilds on pageant wagons on the summer feast of Corpus Christi.
In the York plays the Shipwrights performed the Building of the Ark and the Butchers the Death of Christ.

title: Games and songs
description: Folk football was a rowdy all-comers game that kings banned again and again, in vain; songs like "Sumer is icumen in" survive from the 1200s.

facts.text: Medieval folk football, usually played at Shrovetide or Easter, pitted village against village across fields, streams and narrow streets, and everyone joined in: men and women, rich and poor, clergy too.
Edward II banned football in 1314, and later kings repeated the ban in 1349, 1389, 1401 and 1423, all in vain.
"Sumer is icumen in", a round with the refrain "sing cuckoo", survives in a manuscript made at Reading Abbey in the mid-13th century and now in the British Library.

title: Town dwellers: the first bourgeois
description: Medieval France called a walled-town dweller a bourgeois, as distinct from a peasant; the word later named the middle class.

facts.text: The word bourgeois began in medieval France, meaning someone who lived in a walled town, as distinct from a peasant.
Today the bourgeoisie means the social order dominated by the middle class.

title: Abbasid Baghdad
description: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from Baghdad, founded by al-Mansur in 762 as the Round City.

facts.text: In 750 the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyad caliphs, and the capital later moved to their new city of Baghdad.
In 762 the caliph al-Mansur chose the site of Baghdad for his capital, Madinat al-Salam, built within circular walls: the Round City.

title: The House of Wisdom and the translators
description: Under al-Ma'mun, Baghdad sponsored translation of Greek works into Arabic; the House of Wisdom was a royal library whose scope historians debate.

facts.text: The caliph al-Ma'mun (reigned 813-833) encouraged the translation of ancient Greek works into Arabic.
From about 800 to 1000 a large-scale movement translated Greek works, including Aristotle and Euclid, into Arabic.
Bayt al-Hikmah, the House of Wisdom, was a royal library of the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad; it reached its peak under al-Ma'mun.
Often pictured as a great academy, the House of Wisdom's scope is debated: little evidence puts it at the centre of Baghdad's scholarship.

title: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
description: Al-Khwarizmi, working at the House of Wisdom, wrote the book on al-jabr that named algebra; his Latin name gave us algorithm.

facts.text: Al-Khwarizmi (about 780-850) worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad.
Around 825 al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on calculation by al-jabr and balancing; its 12th-century Latin translation gave us the word algebra.
Al-jabr, "restoring", meant moving a subtracted term to the other side of an equation; balancing cancelled like terms on both sides.
Al-Khwarizmi's name, rendered in Latin as Algoritmi, gave us the word algorithm.

title: Numbers from India
description: Our digits originated in India and reached Europe through scholars of the Islamic world, with Fibonacci's Liber abaci spreading them after 1202.

facts.text: The Hindu-Arabic numerals we use today originated in India in the 6th or 7th century.
Al-Khwarizmi's arithmetic survives in Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, "Al-Khwarizmi Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning".
The numerals reached Europe about the 12th century through mathematicians of the Islamic world, especially al-Khwarizmi and al-Kindi.
Fibonacci learned calculation from an Arab master in North Africa; his Liber abaci (1202) spread the numerals, then known to few Europeans.
