title: The astrolabe in the Islamic world
description: A Greek instrument that reached the Islamic world by the 8th century, where it found prayer times and the qibla and was refined, as in al-Zarqali's universal astrolabe.

facts.text: The astrolabe, roughly "star-taker" in Greek, probably began around the time of the Greek astronomer Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE.
An astrolabe's rete, a star map, turned over a plate made for one latitude, and a sighting rule measured a star's height to find the time.
The astrolabe reached the Islamic world by the 8th century.
In the Islamic world, astrolabes were used to find the qibla, the direction of Mecca, and the five daily prayer times.
Islamic astronomers refined the astrolabe; in Toledo al-Zarqali (1029-1100) made a universal version needing no separate latitude plates.
Al-Zarqali's universal astrolabe, known as the Saphea Arzachelis, was widely used in medieval Europe.

title: Arabic names in the sky
description: Many bright stars carry names adopted from Arabic, passed to Europe through translations of al-Sufi's 10th-century update of Ptolemy's catalog.

facts.text: Many bright stars, including Aldebaran, Betelgeuse, Vega and Altair, have names adopted from Arabic.
Arab astronomers translated the star descriptions of Ptolemy's Almagest, a Greek star catalog compiled around 150 CE.
In the 10th century the Persian astronomer al-Sufi updated the Almagest with his own catalog, later translated into European languages.
The star name Aldebaran means "the follower", because it follows the Pleiades across the sky.

title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
description: Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980-1037) wrote the Canon of Medicine, translated into Latin in the 12th century and used as a textbook in Europe until the mid-17th century.

facts.text: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara in 980 and died in Hamadan in 1037.
Ibn Sina turned to medicine at 16 and, by his own account, found it "easy".
The Canon of Medicine is in five books, from general principles and simple drugs to diseases and compound remedies.
Gerard of Cremona translated the Canon of Medicine into Latin in the 12th century.
Between 1500 and 1674 some sixty editions of the Canon were published in Europe, mostly for university medical training.
The Canon of Medicine served as a medical textbook in Europe until the mid-17th century.

title: Hospitals of the Islamic world
description: Bimaristans in Baghdad, Damascus, Cordoba and Cairo admitted patients regardless of religion or rank; Qalawun's Cairo hospital treated rich and poor free.

facts.text: Bimaristan, the word for a hospital in the medieval Islamic world, is Persian in origin and means "location of disease".
The caliph Harun al-Rashid (reigned 786-809) founded a bimaristan in Baghdad, and al-Ma'mun founded more hospitals there.
Hospitals at Baghdad, Damascus and Cordoba admitted patients regardless of religious belief, race or social order.
Sultan Qalawun's hospital in Cairo (1284-85) treated rich and poor free of charge, with separate wards for different illnesses.

title: Paper from China
description: Chinese craftsmen made the first paper from rags, first as medicine wrapping in the 2nd century BCE, and by the 3rd and 4th centuries CE wrote everything on it.

facts.text: Chinese craftsmen first made paper from washed rags; its first use, in the 2nd century BCE, was as packaging for medicine.
Within a century paper began to replace bamboo strips for writing, and by the 3rd and 4th centuries CE the Chinese wrote everything on it.

title: Paper's journey west
description: Paper reached Samarkand by trade, papermaking arrived there in 751 (the Talas prisoner story is a legend), Baghdad made paper by the 790s, and Europe had it by the 12th century.

facts.text: Chinese paper moved along the Silk Road into Central Asia before the technology of papermaking did.
Before 712, a ruler at Mount Mugh near Samarkand wrote on imported Chinese paper, reusing sheets already written on one side.
The art of papermaking reached Samarkand, in Central Asia, in 751.
Legend says Chinese craftsmen captured at the Battle of Talas in 751 taught papermaking; most scholars think it moved west earlier.
Paper was being made in Baghdad by the 790s, under the caliph Harun al-Rashid.
Soon scholars all over the Islamic world were copying manuscripts onto paper.
Paper reached Europe through Sicily and Spain by the 12th century.

title: Printing in Tang and Song China
description: Printing was invented under the Tang; the Diamond Sutra (868) is the first known dated printed book, and Bi Sheng made clay movable type around 1041-48.

facts.text: The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907, and the Song dynasty from 960 to 1279.
Printing was invented in China under the Tang, first to spread Buddhist scriptures and later for calendars and dictionaries.
In Chinese woodblock printing, a whole page of text was carved into a single block of wood.
The Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868, is the first known dated printed book.
Around 1041-48 Bi Sheng made movable type from clay and glue hardened by baking, but the idea was not followed up in China.

title: Gunpowder, compasses and paper money
description: Chinese gunpowder was used in fireworks and signals by the 10th century; the Song improved compasses for sea trade and pioneered paper money.

facts.text: Francis Bacon named printing, gunpowder and the compass as inventions that changed the world, never realizing all came from China.
Gunpowder, a mix of saltpetre, sulfur and charcoal, originated in China and was used there in fireworks and signals by the 10th century.
Under the Song, advances in compasses, charts and instruments aided long-distance sea trade.
The Song dynasty pioneered paper money as legal tender, helping a booming commercial economy.
Under the Song, several Chinese cities had populations of more than 1,000,000.

title: Genghis Khan and the Mongol empire
description: Temujin, born about 1162, was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206; his heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history.

facts.text: Temujin, born around 1162, was declared universal ruler, Chinggis (Genghis) Khan, by an assembly of Mongol leaders in 1206.
Genghis Khan died in 1227.
At its peak the Mongol empire ran from the Pacific to the Danube, some 23 million sq km: the largest contiguous land empire ever.

title: The cost of the Mongol conquests
description: Estimates of the dead are rough but enormous: roughly 40 million for Genghis Khan's conquests (Britannica); in 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad.

facts.text: Britannica estimates Genghis Khan's conquests killed roughly 40 million people, especially in China and what is now Iran.
One estimate has China's population falling from about 100 million to 65 million in the Mongol invasions, mostly from ruined livelihoods.
Medieval chroniclers exaggerated Mongol death tolls, but even allowing for that, the invasions devastated Muslim Asia as nothing before.
In 1258 Hulegu, Genghis Khan's grandson, sacked Baghdad, killed the caliph and massacred hundreds of thousands; the Abbasid dynasty fell.
Whatever remained of the House of Wisdom's collection was destroyed in the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258.

title: The Silk Road
description: A network of routes about 6,400 km long, travelled in stages by middlemen; silk went west, wool, gold and silver east, and religions travelled too.

facts.text: The Silk Road, a network of routes linking China with the Mediterranean, was about 6,400 km long.
Few people travelled the entire Silk Road; goods were handled in stages by middlemen.
Along the Silk Road, silk went westward, while wool, gold and silver went east.
Buddhism, from India, and Nestorian Christianity reached China along the Silk Road.

title: The Pax Mongolica
description: In the 13th and 14th centuries Mongol rule revived the Silk Road with unprecedented security, the yam relay stations and paiza passes.

facts.text: In the 13th and 14th centuries the Silk Road was revived under the Mongols.
The Pax Mongolica was a period of relative stability, economic integration and cultural exchange in the 13th and 14th centuries.
Despite the violence of the conquests, merchants, diplomats and scholars could cross Mongol lands with unprecedented security.
The Mongols expanded the yam, a network of postal and supply stations, and merchants with paiza passes had imperial protection.
The Pax Mongolica eased the travels of figures such as Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta.

title: Marco Polo
description: The Venetian Marco Polo spent 1271-95 in Asia, 17 years in China, and dictated his Travels to Rustichello; parts are exaggerated, but evidence shows he was in China.

facts.text: Marco Polo, born in Venice about 1254, set out for Asia in 1271, aged 17 or 18, with his father and uncle.
The Polos reached Kublai Khan's court about 1275; Marco was in Asia from 1271 to 1295, 17 of those years in China.
Captured in 1298 in a war between Venice and Genoa, Polo dictated his story in captivity to Rustichello of Pisa, a writer of romances.
Polo claimed Hangzhou had 12,000 bridges; a later traveller found only 347, suburbs included.
In the 1990s historian Frances Wood argued Polo may not have reached China, as he never mentions the Great Wall, tea or foot-binding.
In 2012 Hans Ulrich Vogel showed that Polo's details of Chinese money, salt and revenues closely match Chinese sources.

title: Ibn Battuta
description: Ibn Battuta of Tangier set out on the hajj in 1325 and travelled some 120,000 km across the Islamic world and beyond, dictating his Rihla to Ibn Juzayy.

facts.text: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1304; in 1325, at 21, he set out on the hajj to Mecca.
Ibn Battuta resolved never to travel any road a second time.
Ibn Battuta served for several years as grand qadi (judge) of Delhi, and in 1342 the sultan made him his envoy to China.
Ibn Battuta's wanderings covered some 120,000 km, a figure hardly surpassed by anyone before the age of steam power.
Ibn Battuta dictated his travels, the Rihla, to the writer Ibn Juzayy, who embellished the simple prose.

title: Knowledge flowing east and west
description: Paper, numerals, Greek learning and medicine moved between China, the Islamic world and Europe; under the Pax Mongolica, inventions went west and Islamic science went east.

facts.text: Under the Pax Mongolica, Chinese papermaking, printing, gunpowder and compass went west; Islamic astronomy, math and medicine went east.

title: Magna Carta, 1215
description: In June 1215 rebel barons forced King John to agree to Magna Carta at Runnymede; its clauses 39 and 40 promised lawful judgment and justice for all.

facts.text: On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede between Windsor and Staines, King John agreed to Magna Carta after rebel barons renounced their allegiance and occupied London.
Clause 39 of the 1215 charter promised that no free man would be imprisoned or stripped of his rights except by the lawful judgment of his equals or the law of the land.
Clause 40 of the 1215 charter promised that the king would not sell, deny or delay justice to anyone.

title: Magna Carta's survival
description: The Pope annulled Magna Carta within ten weeks, but it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three of its clauses are still English law.

facts.text: On 24 August 1215, less than ten weeks after Runnymede, Pope Innocent III, to whom John had submitted his kingdom, annulled Magna Carta as "shameful, demeaning, illegal and unjust".
Fighting resumed in September 1215 and went on until King John died in October 1216.
After John's death the charter was reissued in the name of his young son, Henry III, in 1216 and 1217, and again in 1225 in exchange for a new tax.
Only three clauses of Magna Carta remain in English law: the freedom of the English Church, the ancient liberties of the City of London, and the right to lawful judgment.

title: The first parliaments
description: Parliaments grew from royal councils: León's assembly of 1188 included town representatives; in England the word appears in 1236, towns joined in 1265, the Model Parliament met in 1295 and the Commons sat apart from 1341.

facts.text: The word parliament comes from Old French parlement, "a speaking, talk", from parler, "to speak".
The earliest use of the term Parliament in England, for the king's Great Council, dates from 1236.

UNESCO recognizes the Decreta of León of 1188, from the Spanish kingdom of León, as the oldest documentary evidence of Europe's parliamentary system; elected town representatives sat with the king, church and nobles.
In 1265 Simon de Montfort, in rebellion against Henry III, summoned a parliament that for the first time included representatives of both the counties and the towns.
Edward I's Model Parliament of 1295 brought nobles and bishops together with two knights from each county and two burgesses from each town, the pattern for later parliaments.
In 1341 the knights and burgesses met separately from the nobility and clergy for the first time, forming what became the House of Commons.

title: Parliament and taxes
description: Parliament grew because kings needed its consent to extra taxes to pay for their wars.

facts.text: Parliament grew in the 13th and 14th centuries largely because Edward I and his successors needed its assent to extraordinary taxes to pay for their wars.

title: Common law
description: English common law, consolidated under Henry II, was law common to all England, built from the decisions of the king's courts and followed as precedent.

facts.text: English common law was consolidated under Henry II (1154-1189), whose royal officials travelled the country inquiring into how justice was done.
Common law was law common to all of England, made in the king's courts rather than by local customs, and judges came to follow earlier decisions as precedent.
The common-law system that grew in England is also used in the United States and most Commonwealth countries.

title: The first juries
description: Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) created juries that named suspects; after 1215, when ordeals ended, juries also came to decide guilt.

facts.text: Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) had juries of 12 men from each hundred, a district of a county, and 4 from each township report crimes and name suspects to the king's travelling judges.
The presenting jury of the Assize of Clarendon, which decided who should be accused rather than who was guilty, was the ancestor of the grand jury.
After the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 withdrew priests from trials by ordeal, England turned to juries to decide guilt, building on its existing jury of presentment.

title: Trial by ordeal
description: Ordeals of hot iron and cold water asked God to reveal guilt; the Church's 1215 ban on priests blessing them ended them in England.

facts.text: A trial by ordeal judged an accusation by a physical test, on the belief that the outcome would reveal the judgment of God; fire and water were the most common.
In the ordeal of hot iron, the accused held a red-hot iron; the wound was bandaged and checked three days later, and a clean, healing wound meant innocence.
In the ordeal of cold water, an accused person who sank was judged innocent, because the water had accepted them; floating meant guilt.
Priests blessed the water or iron used in ordeals; in 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council forbade anyone to give that blessing.

title: Trial by combat
description: In trial by combat the two sides or their champions fought, trusting God to give victory to the right; it came to England with the Normans and was abolished only in 1819.

facts.text: In trial by combat the two parties, or champions fighting for them, fought on the belief that God would give victory to the side in the right; women, children, clergy and the old or infirm could name a champion.
Trial by combat came into English law after the Norman Conquest.
Trial by battle stayed in English law until Parliament abolished it in 1819, after a defendant claimed it in the case of Ashford v Thornton in 1818.

title: The Hundred Years' War
description: England and France fought on and off from 1337 to 1453, 116 years; England ended with only Calais.

facts.text: The Hundred Years' War between England and France ran from 1337 to 1453, an on-and-off struggle broken by truces.
Despite its name, the Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453.
The name Hundred Years' War was given later by historians; people at the time did not call it that.
By 1453 England had lost all its lands in France except Calais, which it held until 1558.

title: Why the Hundred Years' War began
description: Edward III claimed the French crown through his mother, and English kings held Gascony as vassals of the French king.

facts.text: When Charles IV of France died without a son in 1328, his nephew Edward III of England claimed the French throne through his mother Isabella, Charles's sister, but the French chose Philip of Valois.
England's kings held Gascony, in southwest France, as vassals of the French king, which gave France frequent excuses to interfere there.

title: The longbow at Crécy
description: At Crécy in 1346 English longbowmen, shooting far faster than crossbows, broke repeated French charges.

facts.text: At Crécy on 26 August 1346, Edward III's English army defeated the French.
At Crécy, Italian crossbowmen opened the French attack and were routed by English archers, whose longbows could shoot about three times as fast as crossbows.
At Crécy, some 15 or 16 French attacks were each cut down by the English archers.
The size of the armies at Crécy is disputed: estimates run from about 12,000 to 16,000 English and from about 25,000 to 35,000 French.

title: Agincourt
description: At Agincourt in 1415 Henry V's archers, behind stakes on a narrow muddy field, beat a larger French army; the size of the armies is debated.

facts.text: At Agincourt on 25 October 1415, Henry V's English army defeated a larger French army in a battle that probably lasted no more than three hours.
At Agincourt the English stood on a recently ploughed field narrowed by woods, with sharpened stakes in front of the archers, and the French advanced through mud.
Traditional estimates put the English at Agincourt at about 6,000 and the French at 20,000 to 30,000.
Historian Anne Curry, working from muster rolls and financial records, estimates about 8,500 English against around 12,000 French at Agincourt.
Anne Curry argues that the huge French armies once claimed at Agincourt could not have fitted on the battle site.

title: Joan of Arc's rise
description: A farmer's daughter who heard saints' voices, Joan helped lift the siege of Orléans and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims in 1429.

facts.text: Joan of Arc was born about 1412, the daughter of a tenant farmer at Domrémy in eastern France.
Joan believed she was guided by the voices of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, who told her to help the dauphin Charles and drive out the English.
In May 1429 Joan helped lift the English siege of Orléans.
On 17 July 1429 Charles VII was crowned at Reims, with Joan near the altar holding her banner.

title: Joan of Arc's trial
description: Captured in 1430, Joan was tried by a church court at Rouen; the record preserves her answers, including her escape from the grace-of-God trap. She was burned in 1431 and cleared in 1456.

facts.text: In 1430 Burgundian troops, allies of the English, captured Joan at Compiègne and handed her over to the English.
From January 1431 Joan was tried by a church court at Rouen, presided over by Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais.
Joan's trial is unusually well documented for a medieval trial: the record preserves the judges' questions and her answers.
Asked whether she knew she was in God's grace, Joan faced a trap: the Church held that no one could know, so yes sounded like heresy and no like admitting guilt.
On 24 February 1431 Joan answered: "If I am not, may God place me there; if I am, may God so keep me."
After recanting in May 1431, Joan was found wearing men's clothes again, and the judges declared her a relapsed heretic.
Joan was burned at the stake in Rouen on 30 May 1431, aged about 19.
A retrial authorised by Pope Callixtus III annulled Joan's sentence in 1455-56, and she was made a saint in 1920.

title: How Robin Hood grew
description: Robin Hood is known from rhymes and ballads, not records; Marian and his noble rank were added centuries later.

facts.text: Robin Hood may never have been anything but a legend; attempts to link him to real people lack solid support.
The earliest literary mention of Robin Hood is in the poem Piers Plowman (about 1377), where a lazy priest knows "rhymes of Robin Hood" better than his prayers.
The earliest surviving Robin Hood ballad, Robin Hood and the Monk, dates from about 1450.
Maid Marian is not in the medieval Robin Hood ballads; she came from a separate shepherd-and-shepherdess love story that merged with the legend in the 16th century.
Anthony Munday's plays of 1598-99 turned Robin into a dispossessed earl loyal to King Richard, the noble outlaw of later stories.

title: How King Arthur grew
description: Arthur first appears in the Historia Brittonum (about 830) as a winner of 12 battles against the Saxons; Geoffrey of Monmouth, Chrétien de Troyes and Malory built him into the legend.

facts.text: Scholars have not been able to show that King Arthur was based on a person who really existed.
The earliest known reference to Arthur is in the Historia Brittonum, compiled in Wales around 800 to 830, which lists 12 battles he fought against the Saxons.
Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain (1135-38) made Arthur a glorious king who defeated a Roman army; some of it was plain invention.
In the late 12th century the French poet Chrétien de Troyes introduced the Grail quest and the love of Lancelot and Guinevere.
Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur, from the late 15th century, passed the Arthur legend on to English readers.

title: The Holy Roman Empire
description: A German-centred empire, often dated from Otto I's crowning in 962 to 1806, whose name Voltaire mocked as neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.

facts.text: In 1756 the French writer Voltaire wrote that the Holy Roman Empire was "neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire".
In 962 the German king Otto I was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope John XII, the usual starting point of the Holy Roman Empire.
The word "Holy" joined the empire's name in 1157, and the full title "Holy Roman Empire" was in use from 1254.
The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806, when Francis II gave up the imperial title after Napoleon's rise.

title: Electing an emperor
description: Holy Roman Emperors were elected; the Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the electors at seven, and the empire became a loose federation.

facts.text: Holy Roman Emperors were elected; the Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the electors at seven: the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier and the rulers of Bohemia, the Palatinate, Saxony and Brandenburg.
By the 16th century the Holy Roman Empire had become a loose federation of lands.

title: Kings under law by 1450
description: By 1450 English kings had repeatedly reconfirmed Magna Carta, and Parliament used those reconfirmations to assert the king's duty to uphold the rule of law.

facts.text: Modern research has found as many as 44 reaffirmations of Magna Carta, the last in 1423.
In 1297 Magna Carta was recorded in the Statute Rolls for the first time.
By the 14th century, Parliament's regular reconfirmation of Magna Carta was a public event asserting the king's duty to uphold the rule of law.

title: The Great Famine of 1315
description: Torrential rain from 1315 ruined harvests across northern Europe, causing the worst European famine by share of population.

facts.text: Torrential rain struck France from April 1315 and England from May 1315, and the harvests failed.
Tree-ring records of past weather show the growing seasons of 1314 to 1316 were the fifth wettest in Europe between 1300 and 2012.
The Great Famine ranks as the worst European famine in deaths as a share of the population.
In England, wheat that sold for five shillings in 1313 fetched as much as forty shillings by 1315.
The Great Famine gripped northern Europe from Ireland to Poland and from Scandinavia to central France, and full recovery took until 1322.

title: Why the famine was so bad
description: Historian William Chester Jordan shows how animal diseases, repeated harvest failures, volatile prices and war worsened the weather's damage.

facts.text: Historian William Chester Jordan shows the famine was worsened by animal diseases, repeated harvest failures, volatile prices and war that disrupted food supplies.

title: How the Black Death reached Europe
description: The plague began in Central Asia, struck the Mongol siege of Caffa in 1346, and Genoese ships carried it to Messina in October 1347, from where it spread across Europe by 1350.

facts.text: Plague DNA from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, with tombstones dated 1338 and 1339, points to Central Asia as the Black Death's source.
In 1346 a Mongol army under Janibeg besieging Caffa, an Italian trading port in Crimea, was struck by plague.
The chronicler Gabriele de' Mussi wrote that the besiegers catapulted corpses into Caffa, though he was probably not there to see it.
From Caffa, Genoese ships carried the plague west to Mediterranean ports.
Ships brought the plague to Messina, in Sicily, in early October 1347.
The plague spread from Sicily (1347) to Italy, Spain and France (1348), Germany and the Low Countries (1349), and Scandinavia and the Baltic (1350).

title: The Black Death's death toll
description: Death tolls are estimates: most put Black Death deaths at about 30-50% of Europe's population in 1347-1351, some higher; England lost around a third by 1349.

facts.text: Death tolls are estimates: most put Black Death deaths at about 30-50% of Europe's population between 1347 and 1351.
Historian Ole Benedictow calculated a higher toll: about 60% of Europe's population.
In England, the Black Death had killed around a third of the population by 1349.

title: What caused the plague
description: Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, confirmed for the Black Death by ancient DNA from victims' teeth; bubonic plague spreads by flea bites, pneumonic plague person to person.

facts.text: Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and today can be cured with antibiotics if treated quickly.
In 2011 scientists sequenced the Black Death bacterium's genome from teeth in a 14th-century plague pit at East Smithfield, London: it was Yersinia pestis.
Plague usually spreads to people through bites from infected rodent fleas.
Bubonic plague causes swollen, painful lymph nodes called buboes; pneumonic plague infects the lungs and is the only form that spreads person to person, through respiratory droplets.

title: Rats or people? The transmission debate
description: The rat-flea story is challenged by Dean et al. (2018), whose human flea and louse model fit death records better in seven of nine outbreaks; the question is still debated.

facts.text: A 2018 study led by Katharine Dean found that human fleas and body lice fit the death records better than rats in seven of nine European plague outbreaks from 1348 to 1813.
Rats spread plague in modern outbreaks, and how the medieval plague spread between people is still debated.

title: Plague, wages and work
description: With workers scarce after the Black Death, wages rose and labour services gave way to wages and rents; England's Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to freeze wages.

facts.text: After the Black Death, the labour shortage pushed up wages for artisans and other workers, and landowners swapped labour services for wages or money rents.
With land cheap and wages high, many survivors of the plague enjoyed a higher standard of living.
England's Statute of Labourers of 1351 tried to freeze wages at pre-plague levels and stop workers moving to find better pay.

title: Faith, fear and blame
description: The plague drove flagellant processions and the false blaming of Jews, who were massacred across Europe, as at Strasbourg in 1349, though they died of plague too.

facts.text: During the Black Death, groups of flagellants, believing the plague a punishment from God, marched through towns whipping themselves to atone for sins and calling on people to repent.
Jews were falsely accused of causing the Black Death by poisoning wells, and many were killed by mobs or burned.
In Strasbourg on 14 February 1349, about 2,000 Jews were burned, a city chronicler recorded; the plague only reached Strasbourg that summer.
Jews were dying of the plague too, yet the accusation was widely believed.
At Avignon, Pope Clement VI protected Jews, who were not burned there.

title: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381
description: Angered by the Statute of Labourers and set off by the poll tax of 1380, rebels led by Wat Tyler and inspired by John Ball marched on London in 1381.

facts.text: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was one of the largest popular uprisings in medieval Europe.
The revolt was set off by the unpopular poll tax of 1380, on top of grievances over the Statute of Labourers' wage limits.
The priest John Ball, excommunicated for preaching a classless society, asked: "When Adam dug and Eve spun, who was then a gentleman?"
Led by Wat Tyler, the rebels entered London on 13 June 1381; King Richard II was 14.

title: How the revolt ended
description: Richard II promised to abolish serfdom at Mile End; Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield, the promises were forgotten, but no poll tax was levied for over 250 years.

facts.text: At Mile End, Richard II promised the rebels the abolition of serfdom and forced labour.
At Smithfield, the mayor of London, William Walworth, cut Wat Tyler down in front of the king.
The king's promises were promptly forgotten, but no further poll tax was levied for more than 250 years.

title: Gunpowder reaches Europe
description: Black powder, thought to originate in China, was used in European firearms from the 14th century, moving the power of weapons from muscle to chemistry; giant guns like Mons Meg followed.

facts.text: Black powder, a mix of saltpetre, sulfur and charcoal, is thought to have originated in China, where it was used in fireworks and signals by the 10th century.
Black powder was adopted for firearms in Europe from the 14th century.
Before gunpowder, weapons depended on muscle power.
Mons Meg, a six-tonne siege gun made in Mons and given to King James II of Scotland in 1457, could fire a 150 kg gunstone up to 3.2 km.

title: Guns end the age of castles
description: Firearms improved so fast in the 15th and 16th centuries that French guns took castle after castle in Italy in 1494, ending the age of the medieval castle.

facts.text: When French troops marched through Italy in 1494, their guns reduced castle after castle with astonishing speed.
Firearms developed so fast in the 15th and 16th centuries that military architecture changed completely and the age of the medieval castle ended.

title: The siege of Constantinople, 1453
description: Sultan Mehmed II, aged 21, used Urban's great cannon against the walls and hauled ships overland past the Golden Horn chain in the siege of April to May 1453.

facts.text: Sultan Mehmed II, born in 1432, was 21 when he besieged Constantinople in 1453.
Mehmed hired the Hungarian gunsmith Urban to build cannon powerful enough to bring down Constantinople's walls, and the cannon opened a breach.
The Ottoman bombardment began on 6 April 1453, and the final assault came in the early hours of 29 May.
Between 60,000 and 80,000 Ottoman soldiers with 69 cannon faced only 6,000 to 7,000 trained defenders.
To get past the chain across the Golden Horn, Mehmed hauled smaller ships overland on an oiled wooden ramp; by 22 April they were inside.

title: After the fall of Constantinople
description: Constantine XI died, Hagia Sophia became a mosque, Mehmed moved his capital from Edirne to Constantinople, and the Byzantine Empire ended.

facts.text: The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI, is reported to have been killed, either fighting near the breach or fleeing.
After taking the city, Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia and converted it into a mosque.
Mehmed moved his capital from Edirne to Constantinople, and the Byzantine Empire came to an end.

title: The Wars of the Roses
description: From 1455 to 1485 the houses of Lancaster and York, both descended from Edward III, fought for England's crown; the rose name came long afterward.

facts.text: The Wars of the Roses (1455-1485) were fights for England's throne between the houses of Lancaster and York, both descended from Edward III.
King Henry VI suffered spells of madness, and powerful nobles with private armies spread lawlessness; the first battle came at St Albans in 1455.
The wars were named long afterward, from the supposed badges of the two sides: the white rose of York and the red rose of Lancaster.

title: Bosworth and the Tudors
description: Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth in 1485, married Elizabeth of York and founded the Tudor dynasty; Richard's skeleton was found in Leicester in 2012.

facts.text: On 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth Field, where Richard was killed.
As Henry VII, he married Elizabeth of York in 1486, uniting the rival claims and founding the Tudor dynasty.
In September 2012 a University of Leicester team found a skeleton with a curved spine and battle wounds under a car park on the site of the Grey Friars church.
In 2013, with DNA matching living relatives of his family line, the university announced it was Richard III beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Where the Ottomans came from
description: Founded about 1300 by Osman I, the Ottomans entered the Balkans as Byzantine allies, took Gallipoli in 1354 and built the Janissaries.

facts.text: The Ottoman dynasty and empire were founded about 1300 by Osman I, a Turkmen chief near Bursa in Anatolia; the name Ottoman comes from Osman.
Osman's son Orhan crossed into the Balkans as ally of the future Byzantine emperor John VI, married his daughter Theodora, and in 1354 took Gallipoli as a permanent foothold in Europe.
From the late 14th century the Janissaries, the first modern standing army in Europe, were recruited from Christian boys of the Balkans converted to Islam.
The Ottoman state lasted more than 600 years, until 1922, and at its height reached the gates of Vienna.

title: Near-collapse and recovery
description: In 1402 Timur defeated Bayezid I at Ankara and split Ottoman lands among his sons; after civil war Mehmed I reunited them in 1413.

facts.text: In 1402 Timur, a conqueror from Central Asia, defeated Sultan Bayezid I near Ankara, and Bayezid died in captivity.
Timur split the Ottoman lands among Bayezid's sons, who fought each other until Mehmed I reunited them in 1413.

title: Crisis and resilience in the late Middle Ages
description: Famine, plague, financial collapse and war cut Europe's population for a time to about half of its 70 million of 1300, yet Europe proved resilient and recovered.

facts.text: Historians of the 15th and 16th centuries described the Middle Ages as sinking into old age, a view backed by disasters such as the famine of 1315 and the Black Death.
Famine, plague, war and financial collapse cut Europe's population for a time to about half of the 70 million people of 1300.
Many historians now stress Europe's resilience, which explains its recovery in the late 14th and 15th centuries.

title: Gutenberg's movable type
description: Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg printed with reusable metal letters and a press, producing the Gutenberg Bible about 1455.

facts.text: Johannes Gutenberg developed printing in Strasbourg and Mainz; by about 1450 his experiments had reached a considerable degree of refinement.
Gutenberg cast type from a metal alloy that melted readily and cooled quickly into durable, reusable letters.
Gutenberg's press, which applied firm, even pressure, was likely adapted from presses used for wine, oil or paper.
The Gutenberg 42-line Bible was printed in Mainz in 1454/1455, in a run of perhaps as many as 180 copies, about a quarter of them on vellum.

title: From thousands of books to millions
description: Printing turned Europe's few thousand manuscript books into more than 9 million printed books by 1500, in editions larger than whole monastic libraries.

facts.text: Before printing, manuscript books in Europe could be counted in thousands; by 1500, after only 50 years of printing, there were more than 9,000,000 books.
Early printed editions usually ran to about 250 copies; the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius printed editions of 1,000.

title: The Renaissance begins in Italy
description: The Renaissance, 'rebirth', began in 14th-century Italy as a revival of classical learning, funded by rich city-states and families such as Florence's Medici.

facts.text: Renaissance is French for 'rebirth'; it began in Italy in the 14th century, marked by a surge of interest in Classical scholarship and values.
Humanism, pioneered by Petrarch, sought to recover the learning of ancient Greece and Rome.
Italy's wealthy city-states funded the Renaissance; in Florence, merchant families led by the Medici paid to build and decorate palaces, churches and monasteries.

title: Humanists hunt for lost classics
description: Humanists such as Poggio Bracciolini recovered ancient texts from medieval monastery libraries, and Poggio's humanist handwriting became the model for roman type.

facts.text: On expeditions in 1417 to Fulda, St. Gall and other monasteries, the Italian humanist Poggio Bracciolini recovered lost texts, including Lucretius's poem De rerum natura.
Poggio found two unknown orations of Cicero at Cluny in 1415, and at St. Gall in 1416 the first complete text of Quintilian's handbook on oratory.
Poggio developed the humanist script, a round, formal handwriting based on the medieval Caroline minuscule, which became the prototype of roman type.

title: The caravel
description: The Portuguese developed the caravel, a light ship with triangular lateen sails that could sail against the wind, to explore Africa's coast.

facts.text: The Portuguese developed the caravel, a light ship with two or three masts and triangular lateen sails, to explore Africa's coast.
The caravel's great advantage was that it could sail against the wind, which exploring a coast with contrary winds required.
Two of Columbus's three ships in 1492, the Nina and the Pinta, were caravels.
In the 12th century mariners in China and Europe discovered, apparently independently, that a floating lodestone points toward the polestar.

title: Portugal's voyages around Africa
description: Prince Henry sponsored voyages down West Africa for gold and enslaved people; Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and da Gama reached India in 1498.

facts.text: Prince Henry of Portugal (1394-1460), called 'the Navigator', never went on a voyage of exploration himself; he sponsored them.
Henry's voyages down West Africa sought a share of its trade in gold and in enslaved people; in 1441 a caravel returned with gold dust and enslaved Africans.
In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias led the first European expedition to round the Cape of Good Hope, opening a sea route to Asia.
Vasco da Gama was the first to sail from Europe to India around the Cape of Good Hope, reaching Calicut in May 1498.

title: Columbus's voyage of 1492
description: Funded by Ferdinand and Isabella, Columbus sailed from Palos in August 1492 and reached the Bahamas on October 12, believing he was in Asia.

facts.text: Funded by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos on August 3, 1492, with three ships.
On October 12, 1492, Columbus reached the Bahamas, believing he had arrived in Asia.

title: Columbus and the round Earth
description: Educated Europeans already knew the Earth was a sphere; Columbus's error was underestimating its size. The flat-Earth story comes from Washington Irving's 1828 biography.

facts.text: Columbus's contemporaries never thought the world was flat: educated Europeans had known it was a sphere since at least the early 7th century.
Columbus's real error was size: he believed Earth was much smaller than it is and Asia much farther east.
The story that Columbus proved the Earth round comes from Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus, which filled gaps with invented detail.

title: What 1492 cost the Taino
description: Columbus enslaved Taino people, and enslavement, starvation and imported disease reduced the Taino from perhaps one or two million to a few thousand by 1520.

facts.text: The Taino, the Indigenous people Columbus met in the Caribbean, were its most numerous people and may have numbered one or two million at contact.
Columbus decided the Taino would make ideal slaves: in 1495 he shipped 500 of them to Spain, and some 200 died on the voyage.
In 1495 Columbus's forces killed and captured many Taino on Hispaniola, and he forced others near the gold mines to pay tribute in gold or cotton.
Enslavement, starvation and disease brought by the Spanish reduced the Taino to a few thousand by 1520.
Older accounts called Columbus the 'discoverer' of the New World, though Native Americans lived there long before; historians now stress the slave trade and imported disease his voyages unleashed.

title: The empire of Mali
description: Founded by Sundiata about 1230, Mali grew rich on the gold and salt trade and under Mansa Musa took in Timbuktu and Gao.

facts.text: The Catalan Atlas, made in Majorca in 1375, shows Mansa Musa of Mali holding a golden ball and calls him the richest and noblest king of the land.
Sundiata founded the empire of Mali on the upper Niger River around 1230, and its armies secured gold-bearing lands to the south.
Mali grew rich by controlling the trade in gold and salt.
Under Mansa Musa (mansa means emperor), Mali took in the trading cities of Timbuktu and Gao; Musa said it took a year to travel across his empire.
Back from Mecca, Mansa Musa had the Great Mosque (Djinguereber) of Timbuktu built, and the city grew into a center of Islamic scholarship.

title: Mansa Musa's hajj
description: On his 1324 pilgrimage, Mansa Musa gave away so much gold in Cairo that, al-Umari reported, its value fell for about twelve years; 'richest person ever' is a popular claim that cannot be measured.

facts.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa made the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, passing through Cairo with a huge caravan.
The Arab historian al-Umari, who came to Egypt a few years after the pilgrimage, reported that Musa left no court emir or royal official without the gift of a load of gold.
According to al-Umari, so much gold was spent in Egypt that its value fell and had still not recovered about twelve years later.
Mansa Musa is popularly called the richest person in history, but historians say his wealth is impossible to calculate accurately.

title: The stone city of Great Zimbabwe
description: Built by ancestors of the Shona between the 11th and 15th centuries, Great Zimbabwe's mortarless stone walls ruled a kingdom rich from the gold trade with the Indian Ocean coast.

facts.text: The country of Zimbabwe takes its name from the site; zimbabwe is a Shona word meaning 'stone houses'.
Great Zimbabwe was built by ancestors of the Shona people and flourished between the 11th and 15th centuries.
At its height Great Zimbabwe supported a population of 10,000 to 20,000.
The Great Enclosure, the largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa, has granite walls laid without mortar, standing 32 feet (about 10 metres) high in places.
Great Zimbabwe prospered on cattle, crops and the trade of gold with the coast of the Indian Ocean.
Excavations at Great Zimbabwe found goods from distant lands: Syrian glass, Chinese celadon dishes and Persian faience bowls.

title: Who built Great Zimbabwe: the colonial myth
description: Colonial-era Europeans falsely credited Great Zimbabwe to foreigners; archaeology in 1905 and 1929 showed it was medieval and African, yet Rhodesia's government censored the truth.

facts.text: Late 19th-century Europeans refused to credit Africans with Great Zimbabwe: Karl Mauch linked it to the Queen of Sheba, and Theodore Bent to Phoenicians or Arabians.
In 1905 the archaeologist David Randall-MacIver found the ruins were medieval and of exclusively African origin; Gertrude Caton-Thompson confirmed this in 1929.
From 1965 to 1980, Rhodesia's ruling party censored books and other material on Great Zimbabwe, and archaeologists who spoke of its African origin were punished.

title: The Maya
description: Maya cities flourished in the Classic period (about 250-900), with the only true writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas.

facts.text: Maya civilization flourished in its Classic period, about 250 to 900, with many cities; the great lowland cities were abandoned around 900.
Maya hieroglyphic writing was the only true writing system developed in the pre-Columbian Americas.
Maya people still live in the region today, and millions speak Mayan languages.

title: The Aztecs and Tenochtitlan
description: The Mexica (Aztecs) founded Tenochtitlan about 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco; estimates of its 1519 population range from about 50,000 to 400,000.

facts.text: The Mexica, or Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco, linked to the mainland by causeways.
Estimates of Tenochtitlan's population in 1519 range from about 50,000 to about 400,000.
Without reliable censuses, ancient city populations are rough estimates, usually made from a city's known area and likely housing density.

title: The Inca
description: The Inca ruled from Ecuador to central Chile with great roads and knotted-cord records (quipu); about 12 million people lived in the empire in 1532, though estimates vary.

facts.text: The Inca empire stretched along the Andes and the Pacific coast from northern Ecuador to central Chile.
Two Inca roads ran north-south, each about 3,600 km long, and relay runners carried messages as quipu, knotted cords.
The Inca empire's population in 1532 is commonly estimated at about 12 million, though estimates vary.

title: Cahokia
description: Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, was the largest city north of Mexico, flourishing about 950-1350 with an estimated 8,000 to 40,000 people.

facts.text: Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, was the largest urban center north of Mexico and flourished from about 950 to 1350.
Estimates of Cahokia's peak population range from 8,000 to 40,000.
Cahokia's Monks Mound rises 30 meters, the largest prehistoric earthen structure in the Western Hemisphere.

title: When the Middle Ages ended
description: Historians end the Middle Ages at different dates, most often 1453 (Constantinople falls), 1492 (Columbus) or 1517 (Luther), all near 'about 1500'.

facts.text: Historians give different end dates for the Middle Ages, most often 1453, 1492 or 1517.
On May 29, 1453, the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire, an event long held to mark the end of the Middle Ages.
In 1517 Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg began the Reformation, which reshaped Western Christianity.
Luther's ideas were printed and reprinted within weeks and read across Europe; print was the catalyst of the Reformation.

title: Medieval inventions we still use
description: Eyeglasses (Italy, about 1290) and mechanical tower clocks are medieval inventions still in daily use.

facts.text: Eyeglasses were first made in Italy, most probably in Pisa, around 1290; the first ones had convex lenses to help farsighted people.
In a sermon of 1306, the friar Giordano da Pisa said the art of making eyeglasses was not yet twenty years old, and that he had spoken to its discoverer.

The first clearly recorded mechanical clocks were large weight-driven machines in towers; they struck the hours rather than showing them. England's oldest surviving one, at Salisbury Cathedral, dates from 1386.
The word clock comes from Medieval Latin clocca, 'bell'.
